We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$  to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.

First suppose that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$.
Let $h$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. We extend $h$ as follows. First we map the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ by the identity. This will ensure surjectivity. We then map the various copies of $\Cylm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$. This is always possible: because $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$, we have $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\HC_0])=V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ due to Lemma~\ref{lem:spillage}. Hence, if $h(x)=y$ for two vertices $x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ and $y\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, we can always find a retraction of the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\HC_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that maps $x$ to $y$, and we mimic this retraction on the corresponding subgraph in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$. The crucial observation is that this can be done independently for each vertex in $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$, as two vertices of different copies of $\Cylm$ are only adjacent if they both belong to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$.
This leads to a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.

Now suppose that there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$  to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
If $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$, then by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}, $|h(\Cylm)|=1$ for all copies of $\Cylm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$. This means that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'')|=1$ and $h$ is not surjective, a contradiction. Now, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<m$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=m$ and indeed $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ for some isomorphism~$i$. 

We claim that $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\HC_0)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. In order to see this, consider a vertex $y\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. 
As $h$ is surjective, there exists a vertex~$x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'')$ with $h(x)=y$. By construction, $x$ belongs to some copy of $\DCm$, and thus also belongs to some copy of $\DCm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\HC_0)$.
We can extend $i^{-1}$ to an isomorphism from the copy of $\Cylm$  (which has $i(\HC_0)$ as its bottom cycle)  in the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\HC_0))$ to the copy of $\Cylm$ (which has $\HC_0$ as its bottom cycle) in the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\HC_0)$.
We define a mapping~$r^*$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\HC_0))$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ by $r^*(u)=h\circ i^{-1}(u)$ if $u$ is on the copy of $\Cylm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\HC_0))$ and $r^*(u)=u$ otherwise. We observe that $r^*(u)=u$ if $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0')$ as $h$ coincides with $i$ on $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. As $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ separates the other vertices of 
the copy of $\Cylm$ from $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$, in the sense that removing $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ would disconnect them, this means that $r^*$ is a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\HC_0))$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. We find that $r^*$ maps $i(x)$ to $h\circ i^{-1}(i(x))=h(x)=y$. Moreover, as $x$ is in some copy of $\DCm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\HC_0)$, we have that $i(x)$ is in some copy of $\DCm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\HC_0))$. We may assume without loss of generality that $i(x)$ belongs to the top copy (cf. Remark~1). We conclude that $y$ always belongs to  $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\HC_0)])$ (cf. Remark~1).

As $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\HC_0)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, we find, by assumption of the lemma, that there exists a retraction $r$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$.  
Now $i^{-1} \circ r \circ h$ ia the desired retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$.  

For contradiction, suppose there is an endomorphism $h$ that maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of itself that is not an automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. In particular, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})|<|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})|$. Choose $h^{-1}$ in the following fashion. We let $h^{-1}$ of $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ be the natural isomorphism of $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ (that inverts the isomorphism given by $h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$). Otherwise we choose $h^{-1}$ arbitrarily, such that $h^{-1}(y)=x$ only if $h(x)=y$. Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a reflexive tournament, containing precisely one edge between distinct vertices, $h^{-1}$ is an isomorphism. Moreover, $h^{-1} \circ h$ is an endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that fixes $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ and that is not an automorphism, a contradiction.

Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be an instance of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction}. 
We build an instance $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}
in the following fashion. First we build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ by augmenting a new copy of $\Cylm$ for every vertex $v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}) \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DCm$ in $\Cylm$ and the bottom copy of $\DCm$ is to be identified with $\HC_0$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ according to the identity function. We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.

First suppose $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Let $r$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Then any extension of~$r$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ is surjective. As $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\HC_0]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ and two vertices in different copies of $\Cylm$ are only adjacent if both of them are in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, we can in fact extend $r$ to a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.

Now suppose there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
If $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$, then Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1} tells us that  $|h(\Cylm)|=1$ for all copies of $\Cylm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$, and then we derive $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')|=1$, contradicting the surjectivity of~$h$.
Moreover, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<m$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=m$ and $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself. 
As $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ is endo-trivial, Lemma~\ref{lem:7} tells us that  the restriction of $h$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ 
is an automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, which we call $\alpha$. The required retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is now given by $\alpha^{-1} \circ h$.

For contradiction, suppose there is an endomorphism $h$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2$ that maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of itself that does not yield an isomorphic copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$. In particular, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)|<|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)|$. We proceed as in the proof of the Lemma~\ref{lem:7}. Choose $h^{-1}$ in the following fashion. We let $h^{-1}$ of $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ be the natural isomorphism of $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ (that inverts the isomorphism given by $h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$). Otherwise we choose $h^{-1}$ arbitrarily, such that $h^{-1}(y)=x$ only if $h(x)=y$. Since 
$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2$ is a reflexive tournament, $h^{-1}$ is an isomorphism. And $h^{-1} \circ h$ is an endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2$ that fixes $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ that does not yield an isomorphic copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$ in $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)$, a contradiction.

Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be an instance of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$-Retraction}.
We will build an instance $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First, take a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ together with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ and build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by identifying these on the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k}$ that they both possess as a subgraph.
We now build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ as follows. 
First we augment $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ with a new copy of $\Cyl_{a_k}$ for every vertex $v\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of 
$\DC^*_{a_k}$ in $\Cyl_{a_k}$, and the bottom copy of $\DC^*_{a_k}$ is to be identified with $\HC_k$ according to the identity function.
Then, for each $i \in [k+1]$, and $v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i}) \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i-1})$, add a copy of $\Cyl_{a_{i-1}}$, where $v$ is identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DC^*_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\Cyl_{a_{i-1}}$ and the bottom copy of $\DC^*_{i-1}$ is to be identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i-1}$ according to the identity map of $\DC^*_{a_{i-1}}$ to $\HC_{i-1}$.
We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$.

First suppose that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$.
Let $h$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k}$. Extend $h$ mapping $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ according to the identity to ensure the final mapping is surjective. Finally, we map the various copies of $\Cyl_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ in any suitable fashion, which will always exist due to our assumptions and the fact that $\mathrm{Spill}_{a_{k}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k},\HC_{k}]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})$, which follows from our assumption that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:spillage}.

Now suppose that if there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$.
Suppose that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$. Then 
$|h(\Cyl_{a_0})|=1$
 by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}. Now we follow the chain of spills to deduce that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})|=1$, which is not possible.
Now, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<a_0$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. 
Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|$ and indeed $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. We now apply Lemma~\ref{lem:8} as well as our assumed endo-trivialities to derive that $h$ in fact maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ by the isomorphism $i$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_{k}$. Since $h$ is surjective, we can deduce that $\mathrm{Spill}_{a_k}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_k,i(\HC_{k})]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})$
in the same way as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{prop:main1}.
 and so there exists a retraction $r$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_k$.  Now $i^{-1} \circ r \circ h$ gives the desired retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$.   

Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be an instance of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$-Retraction}.
We build an instance $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$-Colouring}
in the following fashion. Build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by, for each $i \in [k+1]$, and $v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i}) \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i-1})$, adding a copy of $\Cyl_{a_{i-1}}$, where $v$ is identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DC^*_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\Cyl_{a_{i-1}}$ and the bottom copy of $\DC^*_{i-1}$ is to be identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i-1}$ according to the identity map of $\DC^*_{a_{i-1}}$ to $\HC_{i-1}$.
We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$.

First suppose that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$.
Let $h$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. Then we can extend $h$ by mapping $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ in some suitable fashion, which is possible due to the spill assumptions.

Now suppose that there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. 
Suppose that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$. Then $|h(\Cyl_{a_0})|=1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}. Now we follow the chain of spills to deduce that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})|=1$, a contradiction. 
Now, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<a_0$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. 
Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|$ and indeed $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. We now apply Lemma~\ref{lem:8} as well as our assumed endo-trivialities to derive that $h$ in fact maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ by the isomorphism $i$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$, which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_{k}$. Now we can deduce, via Lemma~\ref{lem:7}, that $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})$ is an automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$, which we call $\alpha$. The required retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to 
$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ 
is now given by $\alpha^{-1} \circ h$.

As $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is is a strongly connected reflexive tournament, which has more than one vertex by our definition, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not transitive.
Note that {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction}
 is \NP-complete, since non-transitive reflexive tournaments omit Taylor polymorphisms~\cite{larose2006taylor}, following Theorem~\ref{thm:ret-hardness}. Thus, if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is endo-trivial, the result follows from Lemma~\ref{prop:main1} (note that we could also have used Corollary~\ref{c-main}).

Suppose $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not endo-trivial. Then, by Lemma~\ref{lem:endo-retraction-trivial}, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not retract-trivial either. This means $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ has a non-trivial retraction to some subtournament~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. We may assume
that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ is endo-trivial, as otherwise we will repeat the argument until we find a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ to an endo-trivial subtournament.
 
 
If $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to all isomorphic copies $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ within it, except possibly those for which $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\HC_0)]) \neq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, then the result follows from  Lemma~\ref{prop:main1}. So there is a copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0)$ to which $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ does not retract for which $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\HC_0)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$.
If $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0)$ is endo-trivial, the result follows from Lemma~\ref{prop:main2}. Thus we assume $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0)$ is not endo-trivial and we deduce the existence of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0 \subset \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1 \subset \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ ($\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$ is strictly between $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$) so that $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1,\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0)$ is endotrivial and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$. Now we are ready to break out. Either $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to all isomorphic copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, except possibly for those so that $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1,i(\HC_1)]) \neq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, and we apply Lemma~\ref{prop:main-general1}, or there exists a copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1$, with $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1,i(\HC_1)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, to which it does not retract. Then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1$ contains $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}''_0$ a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}''_0$ so that $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1,\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}''_0)$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}''_0$ are endo-trivial. We now continue iterating this method, which will terminate because our structures are getting strictly larger.

We need to argue that the instances of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}
that we have constructed 
before
can be assumed to be strongly connected. Noting that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ and the gadgets $\Cylm$ are strongly connected, this is clear once we can assume the inputs to our Retraction problems are strongly connected. For 
{\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'$-Retraction},
where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'$ is a strongly connected reflexive tournament, we can surely assume our inputs are strongly connected. If they were not, then we add individual directed paths of length $|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}')|$ between the relevant vertices. This will not affect the truth of an instance and the result follows.

For strongly connected tournaments, the result follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:strongly-connected1}. Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ instead have $k>1$ strongly connected components
$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(1),\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(k)$. 
Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not transitive, one of these strongly connected components, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i)$, must be of size greater than $1$, whereupon we know from Corollary~\ref{cor:strongly-connected2} that
{\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i)$-Colouring}
 is \NP-complete, even when restricted to strongly connected inputs. 
 
 Let us reduce
{\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i)$-Colouring} to {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} 
by taking a strongly connected input $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ for the former and building $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by adding a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ restricted to $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(1)),\ldots,V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i-1))$, where every vertex here has an edge to every vertex of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, and adding a copy of  $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ restricted to $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i+1)),\ldots,V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(k))$, where every vertex there has an edge from every vertex of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$. 
Note that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ has $k$ strongly connected components $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'(1),\ldots, \ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'(k)$, where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'(h)$ is isomorphic to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'(h)$ for $h=1,\ldots,k$, $h\neq i$.
We claim 
that there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i)$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to 
$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.

(Forwards.) Map the additional vertices in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ in the obvious fashion (by the ``identity'') to extend a surjective homomorphism
from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_i$ so that it is surjective from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to
$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.

(Backwards.) 
In any surjective homomorphism $s$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, we have that $s(V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'(i))) \subseteq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i))$ for $i=1,\ldots k$. 

For the transitive case we can say that {\sc \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}-Retraction} is in \NL\ from \cite{DalmauK08}, since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ enjoys the ternary median operation as a polymorphism (this has been observed, inter alia, in \cite{larose2006taylor}). It follows of course that {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is in \NL\ also. The non-transitive case follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:hauptsatz}.

Recall the self-map digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}$, with vertices the self-maps of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, and an edge $(f,g) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ between self-maps $f$ and $g$ if and only if for every edge $(x,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, we have that $(f(x),g(y)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. 
In the self-map digraph, the endomorphisms are precisely the looped vertices.

Consider the homomorphism $\varphi: \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n \rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}$ induced by an $n+1$-ary polymorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ where $n \geq 1$; suppose for a contradiction that the polymorphism depends on all its variables. Then clearly the image of $\varphi$ contains at least two elements, and at least one of these elements is not a constant map.  

\noindent{\bf Claim 0.} {\em The only loops in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}$ are the constant maps 1 and 2 and the identity. }

\noindent {\em Proof of Claim 0}: let $f$ be an endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Then $f$ maps loops to loops. Since $(1,2)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, $f$ can either map both to 1, both to 2 , or fix both. Clearly if it fixes both $f$ is the identity. Otherwise, if $f(1)=f(2)=i$, then $(f(0),i) , (i,f(0)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ so $f(0)=i$. 

Without fear of confusion, we denote the constant maps by 0, 1 and 2. We denote the identity map by $id$.

\noindent{\bf Claim 1.} {\em (a) There are no edges in  $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}$ between the identity and the constant maps; (b) if $(2,f), (f,1) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, then $f=0$; (c) if $c$ is a constant map such that $(f,c),(c,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ then $f = c$. }



\noindent {\em Proof of Claim 1}:  $(2,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $(2,f(i)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ for all $i$ so $f(i) \in \{0,2\}$ for all $i$. Similarly $(f,1)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $f(i) \in \{0,1\}$ for all $i$ so (b) follows immediately. To prove (a), observe that any in- or out-neighbour of a constant cannot be surjective since no constant has in- or out-neighbourhood of size 3. For (c), argue again as we just did: $(1,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ means $f(i) \in \{1,2\}$ for all $i$, and $(f,1)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $f(i) \in \{0,1\}$ for all $i$ and hence $f=1$; the proof for $c=2$ is identical.  



\noindent{\bf Claim 2.} {\em If $(f,id),(id,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ then $f = id$. }

\noindent {\em Proof of Claim 2}: Assume that $(f,id),(id,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. If $i$ is a loop then $(i,i)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $(f(i),i),(i,f(i))\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$  thus $f(i) = i$. Now $(0,1)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $(f(0),1)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, and $(2,0)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $(2,f(0))\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ so $f(0)=0$. 


Obviously the loops of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ are precisely the tuples whose coordinates belong to $\{1,2\}$. Call the subdigraph induced by these vertices $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$, and notice it is weakly connected. Then the homomorphism $\varphi$ must map $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$  onto a weakly connected digraph consisting of loops only. By Claim 1 (a) either  (i) $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$ is entirely mapped to $\{id\}$ or (ii) $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$ is mapped by $\varphi$ to the set $\{1,2\}$.

Choose any tuple $X$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ containing a coordinate equal to 0. Then there exist $Y, Z \in W$ such that $(X,Z), (Z,Y), (Y,X) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n)$: indeed, let $Z$ be obtained from $X$ by replacing each  0 entry by 1, fixing all other coordinates, and let $Y$ be obtained from $X$ by replacing each 0 entry by 2, fixing all other coordinates. Thus in case (i) we get that $id = \varphi(Y), (\varphi(Y),\varphi(X)),(\varphi(X),\varphi(Z)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ and $\varphi(Z)=id$ so by Claim 2 $\varphi$ maps all of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ to $id$. remark:
This paper concerns the computational complexity of 
the \emph{surjective homomorphism} problem, also known in the literature as {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} \cite{CiE2017,GolovachPS12} and {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Vertex-Compaction} \cite{VikasAlgorithmica}. This problem requires the homomorphism
to be surjective.
It is a cousin of the \emph{list homomorphism} problem and is even more closely related to the \emph{retraction} and \emph{compaction} problems. Indeed, the {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Compaction} problem, hitherto defined only for graphs~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, takes as input a graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ and asks if there exists a function $f$ from $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ to $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ so that for each non-loop edge $(x,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ (\mbox{i.e.} with $x\neq y$), there exists $u,v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ so that $f(u)=x$ and $f(v)=y$. Thus, compaction can be seen as the \emph{edge-surjective homomorphism} problem.\footnote{Except for the treatment of self-loops, which appears to be an idiosyncrasy that plays no vital role in computational complexity. For some history of the definition see \cite{VikasReflexive}.} The problem {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} takes as input a superstructure~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ and asks whether there is a homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that is the identity on $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. 
The {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} problem is polynomially equivalent with a special type of CSP, CSP$(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}')$, where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'$ is $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ decorated with constants naming the elements of its domain.
 Feder and Vardi~\cite{FederVardi} showed that
the task of classifying the complexities of the retraction problems is equivalent to that for the CSPs. 
Hence, owing to ~\cite{FVproofBulatov,FVproofZhuk}, {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} has now been fully classified.

Nevertheless classification results for {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} have tried to keep pace with similar ones for  {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction}. In \cite{pseudoforests} it is proved, among partially reflexive pseudoforests~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, where the problem {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} splits between P and \NP-complete. A similar classification for {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} over partially reflexive forests can be inferred from the classification for partially reflexive trees in \cite{GolovachPS12}. The quest for a classification for {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Compaction} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} over pseudoforests is ongoing, but for both problems already the reflexive $4$-cycle took some time to classify \cite{JCTBMartinPaulusma,VikasReflexive}, as well as the irreflexive $6$-cycle~\cite{VikasIrreflexive,VikasMFCS}.

Reflexive tournaments form an important subclass of the class of reflexive semicomplete graphs
and are well-understood algebraically~\cite{larose2006taylor}.  
In particular,
the classification for {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a reflexive tournament can be inferred from 
the algebraic characterisation from~\cite{larose2006taylor}: for a reflexive tournament~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, the {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} problem is in NL if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is transitive, and it is \NP-complete otherwise. This raises the question whether the same holds for {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} and whether we can develop algebraic methods further to prove this.
In fact, the algebraic method is by now well known for CSPs and their relatives, including its use with digraphs; see the recent survey \cite{LaroseSurvey17}. However, the algebraic method is not so far advanced for surjective homomorphism problems.
So far it only exists in the work of Chen~\cite{ChenSurHom}, who proved that {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \NP-complete if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ 
has the property that all of its polymorphisms depend only on one variable, that is, are essentially unary. 
Chen's result has not yet been put to work (even on toy open problems) and a key driver for our research has been to find, in the wild, a place for its application.

The \emph{directed path} on $k$ vertices is the digraph with vertices $u_0,\ldots, u_{k-1}$ and edges $(u_i,u_{i+1})$ for $i=0,\ldots,k-2$.
The \emph{directed cycle} on $k$ vertices is obtained from the directed path on $k$ vertices after adding the edge $(u_{k-1},u_0)$.
A digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is \emph{strongly connected} if for all $u,v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ there is a 
directed path 
in $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ from $u$ to $v$ (note that we take this to include the situation $u=v$, but for reflexive graphs the distinction is moot). A digraph is \emph{weakly connected} if its symmetric closure (underlying undirected graph) is connected. A \emph{double-edge} in a digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ consists in a pair of distinct vertices $u,v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, so that $(u,v),(v,u) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. 
A digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is \emph{semicomplete} if for every two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, at least one of $(u,v)$, $(v,u)$ belongs to $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. 
A digraph~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is a \emph{tournament} if for every two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, exactly one of $(u,v)$, $(v,u)$ belongs to $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$.
We demand our tournaments have more than one vertex (to rule out certain trivial cases in proofs). A reflexive tournament $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is \emph{transitive} if for every triple of vertices $u,v,w$ with $(u,v), (v,w)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, also $(u,w)$ belongs to $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$.
 A digraph~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}$ is a \emph{subgraph} of a digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ if $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}) \subseteq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ and $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}) \subseteq E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. It is \emph{induced} if $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}})$ coincides with $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ restricted to pairs containing only vertices of $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}})$. A \emph{subtournament} is an induced subgraph of a tournament (note that this is a fortiori a tournament). All subgraphs we consider in this paper will be induced.

Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be a digraph. An \emph{endomorphism} of~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is a homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to itself. 
 An endomorphism~$e$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is a \emph{constant map} if there exists a vertex $v\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ such that $e(u)=v$ for all $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$.
The \emph{self-map digraph} $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}$ has as its vertices the self-maps of $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, and there is an edge $(f,g) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ between self-maps $f$ and $g$ if and only if for every edge $(x,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, we have that $(f(x),g(y)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. The \emph{endomorphism digraph} $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}}$ is the restriction of the self-map digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}$ to the vertices induced by endomorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$. Note that the self-loops of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}$ are precisely the endomorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, so $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}}$ is reflexive when $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is reflexive. We now make two more observations. 
The first one follows directly from the definition of $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}}$ as well. 
The second one can, for example, be found in Section~5.2 of~\cite{llt}.

We note that every endo-trivial structure is also retract-trivial. However, the reverse implication is not necessarily true: 
in Figure~\ref{fig:Tournament6} we give an example of a structure that is retract-trivial but not endo-trivial.
This example is based on a digraph but is not itself a digraph. It is also possible to construct a retract-trivial digraph that is not endo-trivial~\cite{Si17}, but
on reflexive tournaments both concepts do coincide.
The following lemma is crucial and will be of use in the next section as well.

It is not difficult to construct endo-trivial reflexive tournaments other than reflexive directed cycles.
In the next section though we give a combinatorial \NP-hardness proof for {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} whenever $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is {\it any} non-transitive reflexive tournament. As $\DC^*_3$ is such a digraph, this proof also can be used for the case $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}=\DC^*_3$.
However, it does not extend to {\sc Surjective $\DC^*_k$-Colouring} for $k\geq 4$.

We will use another property, denoted \textbf{$(\dagger)$}, of $\Cylm$, which is that the retractions from $\Cylm$ to its bottom copy of $\DCm$, once propagated through the intermediate copies, induce on the top copy precisely the set of automorphisms of $\DCm$. That is, the top copy of $\DCm$ is mapped isomorphically to the bottom copy, and all such isomorphisms may be realised.
The reason is that in such a retraction, the $(j+1)$th copy may either map under the identity to the $j$th copy, or rotate one edge of the cycle clockwise, 
and $\Cylm$ consists of sufficiently many (namely $m$) copies of $\DCm$.

When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is a reflexive tournament, we may break it up into strongly connected components 
$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}(1),\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}(k)$ so that, for all $i < j \in [k]$, for all $x \in \ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}(i)$ and for all $y \in \ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}(j)$, $(x,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. This is the standard decomposition, inducing a standard order on the connected components, that we will use.

We are not aware of a published classification for {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction}, when $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a partially reflexive digraph of size at most $3$, though we know of one for {\sc List $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} from \cite{FederHellTucker}. Our starting point is therefore

Bearing in mind that membership in \Ptime\ for {\sc List $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} gives this a fortiori for {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}, these sporadic digraphs are the only ones we need to consider. Note that the principal objects of study in \cite{FederHellTucker} are \emph{trigraphs} and the reference to \emph{complement} in that paper's Theorem~3.1 is to trigraph complement, which is different from the various notions of (di)graph complement.

Let $3\mathrm{NRC}$ be the hypergraph with vertex-set $\{r,g,b\}$ and hyperedge-set $\{r,g,b\}\setminus\{(r,g,b),(r,b,g),(g,b,r),(g,r,b),(b,r,g),(b,g,r)\}$. Then {\sc $3$-No-Rainbow-Colouring} is the problem {\sc Surjective $3\mathrm{NRC}$-Colouring}, in which one looks for a surjective colouring of the vertices, such that no hyperedge is rainbow-coloured (\mbox{i.e.} uses all colours). 
We recall that the complexity of this problem is open since it arose (under a different name) in \cite{ColoringMixedHypertrees}, see also Question~3 in~\cite{SurHomSurvey}.
The {\sc Surjective $\DC^*_3$-Colouring} problem is the digraph problem most closely related to {\sc $3$-No-Rainbow-Colouring}. To explain this, 
when looking for digraphs with a similar character to $3\mathrm{NRC}$, we would insist at least that the automorphism group is transitive. This leaves just the reflexive and irreflexive directed $3$-cycles and the reflexive and irreflexive 3-cliques, that is, $3$-cycles with a double edge between every pair of vertices (admittedly, the cycles have only some of the automorphisms of the cliques). 
If~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is the reflexive $3$-clique, then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-{\sc Retraction} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} are trivial. 
If~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is the irreflexive directed $3$-cycle, then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ has a majority polymorphism, which shows that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-{\sc Retraction}, and thus {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} (see Figure~\ref{fig:Anthony}),
can be solved in polynomial time~\cite{Semicomplete}. 
If~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is the irreflexive $3$-clique, then {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \NP-complete, as there exists a straightforward reduction from 3-{\sc Colouring}.
Hence~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}=\DC^*_3$ was indeed the only case for which determining the complexity of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} was not immediately obvious.

For $1 \le T \le n$, let $H^n_{\leq T}$ denote the subset of $\{-1,1\}^n$
consisting of all inputs Hamming weight at most $T$. We use 
$|x|$ to denote the Hamming weight of an input $x \in \{-1,1\}^n$,
so $H^n_{\leq T} = \{x \in \{-1,1\}^n \colon |x| \leq T\}$.

Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \{-1,1\}^n$. The $\varepsilon$-\emph{approximate degree} of a Boolean function $f : \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\}$, denoted $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(f)$, is the least degree of a real polynomial $p : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $|p(x) - f(x)| \le \varepsilon$ for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and $|p(x)| \le 1 + \varepsilon$ for all $x \in \{-1,1\}^n \setminus \mathcal{X}$. We use the term \emph{approximate degree} without qualification to refer to $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f) = \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{1/3}(f)$.

Choose $d = O(\sqrt{T} \log(1/\varepsilon))$ so that $M := T_d(1 + 1/T) + 1\ge 2/\varepsilon$ (as guaranteed by Property 1 of \Cref{lem:cheb}). Define $V_{T, \varepsilon}$ by the following affine transformation of $T_d$:
\[V_{T, \varepsilon}(x) = \left(1  - \frac{1}{M}\right) - \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d\left(1 + \frac{1}{T} - \frac{|x|}{T}\right).\]
 Then for $|x| = 0$, we have 
\[V_{T, \varepsilon}(x) =  \left(1  - \frac{1}{M}\right) - \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d\left(1 + \frac{1}{T}\right) = 0.\]
If $1 \le |x| \le T$, then $1 + 1/T - |x| / T \in [-1, 1]$, so $V_{T, \varepsilon(x)} \in [1-\varepsilon, 1]$. Finally, if $T +1 \le |x| \le N$, then
\[|V_{T, \varepsilon}(x)| \le 1 + \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d(N / T) \le \exp(O(\sqrt{T} \cdot\log N \cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)),\]

Fix any input $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in X^n$, and let $y = (g(x_1), \dots, g(x_n)) \in \{0,1\}^n$. Let $z \in [0, 1]^n$ be defined by $z = (q(x_1), \dots, q(x_n))$. Since $p$ is an $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial for $f$, by the triangle inequality, it suffices to show that $|p(y) - p(z)| \le \delta n$.

Let $Z$ be a random variable on $\{0,1\}^n$ where each $Z_i = 1$ independently with probability $z_i$. Then due to the multilinearity of $p$, we have
\[p(z) = \mathbb{E}[p(Z)] = \Pr[Z =y] \cdot p(y) + \Pr[Z \ne y] \cdot \mathbb{E}[p(Z) | Z \ne y].\]
Since $q$ is a $\delta$-approximating polynomial for $g$, we have $|y_i - z_i| \le \delta$ for every $i \in [n]$.  Hence,
\[\Pr[Z = y] \ge \left(1 - \delta \right)^n \ge 1 - \delta n.\]
Because $p$ is bounded in $[0, 1]$, this implies
\[p(z) \ge (1 - \delta n) \cdot p(y) + 0 \ge p(y) - \delta n\]
and
\[p(z) \le 1 \cdot p(y) + \delta n \cdot 1 = p(y) + \delta n,\]
completing the proof.

We prove the lemma by induction on the number of variables $n$. If $n = 0$, then $p$ is a constant in the interval $[0, 1]$ and the claim is true.

Now suppose the claim is true for $n-1$ variables, and let $p : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ with $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for $x \in \{0,1\}^n$. We begin by decomposing
\[p(x) = (1-x_n) \cdot q_0(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}) + x_n \cdot q_1(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})\]
where $q_0$ and $q_1$ are themselves multilinear polynomials. Since $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for all $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, this is in particular true when $x_n = 0$. Hence $q_0(x') \in [0, 1]$ for all $x' \in \{0,1\}^{n-1}$. Similarly, setting $x_n = 1$ reveals that $q_1(x') \in [0, 1]$ for all $x' \in \{0,1\}^{n-1}$. Now for any $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $x' = (x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})$ we have
\begin{align*}
|p(x)| &= \left| (1 - x_n) \cdot q_0(x') + x_n \cdot q_1(x')\right| \\
&\le |1 - x_n| \cdot |q_0(x')| + |x_n| \cdot |q_1(x')| \\
&\le (|1 - x_n| + |x_n|) \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^{n-1} (|1 - x_i| + |x_i|)
\end{align*}
where the final inequality uses the inductive hypothesis. This proves the claim.

The first two cases are an immediate consequence of \Cref{approxlemma}.

To upper bound the value of $|p_\mathcal{R}(x)|$ for $x\notin \mathcal{P}_\mathcal{R}$, we exploit the structure of $p_\mathcal{R}$ as a multilinear polynomial $w$ of degree $O(\sqrt{N})$ over the variables $z_1,\ldots,z_{|\mathcal{R}|}$, where each $z_r$ is the output of the $r^\mathrm{th}$ polynomial from \Cref{lem:orT}. That is, 
$$z_r = V_{T, 1/(20n)}\left({\mathds{1}}[x_1 = r], \dots, {\mathds{1}}[x_N = r]\right).$$ 
If $b_\mathcal{R}(x)$ range items appear greater than $T$ times, this means that up to $b_\mathcal{R}(x)$ of the variables $z_r$ might take values outside $[0,1]$. 
However, by \Cref{lem:orT}, each of these $b_\mathcal{R}(x)$ variables is still at most ${\exp(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}))}$. By \Cref{lem:real-bound},
\[|w(z)| \le \prod_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \left(|1 - z_r| + |z_r|\right) \le \exp\left(b_\mathcal{R}(x) \cdot \tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right),\]
since each $z_r $ that is in $[0, 1]$ contributes a factor of exactly $1$ to the product, whereas each of the remaining $b_\mathcal{R}(x)$ variables contributes a factor of at most ${\exp(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}))}$ to the product.

To calculate the probability of interest, we begin by analyzing a simplified experiment. Suppose there are $b$ range items $r_1, \dots, r_b$ each appearing greater than $T$ times in $x$. We compute the probability that \emph{none} of the items $r_1, \dots, r_b$ appear in the sample $x_\mathcal{S}$. If $T \ge N - S$, then this probability is zero. Otherwise, by direct calculation, we have for each $i = 1, \dots, b$:
\[\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_i \notin x_\mathcal{S} | r_1 \notin x_\mathcal{S}, \dots, r_{i-1} \notin x_\mathcal{S}] \le \prod_{j = 0}^{S-1} \left(1 - \frac{T}{N-j} \right) \le \left( 1 - \frac{T}{N}\right)^S \le \exp \left(-\frac{ST}{N} \right).\]
Hence the probability that none of $r_1, \dots, r_b$ appear is
\[\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_1 \notin x_\mathcal{S} \land \dots \land r_b \notin x_\mathcal{S}] = \prod_{i  = 1}^b \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_i \notin x_\mathcal{S} | r_1 \notin x_\mathcal{S}, \dots, r_{i-1} \notin x_\mathcal{S}] \le \exp \left(-\frac{bST}{N} \right).\]

Now fix an arbitrary $x$, and let $r_1, \dots, r_{k}$ be the range items appearing greater than $T$ times in $x$. Observe that $k \le N/T$. We estimate the probability of interest by taking a union bound over all subsets of $r_1, \dots, r_k$ of size $b$:
\begin{align*}
\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \ge b] &\le \sum_{Y \subseteq [k] : |Y| = b} \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_{i_j} \notin x_\mathcal{S} \quad \forall j \in Y] \\
& \le \binom{k}{b} \exp \left(-\frac{bST}{N}\right) \\
&\le \exp \left( -\frac{bST}{N} + b \log N\right).
\end{align*}

By renormalizing, it suffices to construction a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that
\begin{align} &\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^T \omega(t) \ge (1 - \delta)\|\omega\|_1  \label{eqn:or-sym-corr-ref}\\
& \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg q < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \label{eqn:or-sym-phd-ref}\\
& |\omega(t)| \le \frac{170 \exp(-c_2 t \sqrt{\delta} /\sqrt{T})\|\omega\|_1}{\delta \cdot t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, \dots, T.\label{eqn:or-sym-decay-ref}\end{align}
 Let $c = \lceil 8 / \delta \rceil$ below. We will freely use the fact that since $\delta \le 1/2$, we have $c \le c^2 / (c-1) \le 10 /\delta$. Let $m = \lfloor \sqrt{T/2c} \rfloor$ and define the set
\[S = \{1, c\} \cup \{2ci^2 : 0 \le i \le m\}.\]
Note that $|S| \ge  c_1 \sqrt{\delta T}$ for some absolute constant $c_1 > 0$. Define the function
\[\omega(t) = \frac{(-1)^{t+(T-m)}}{T!} \binom{T}{t} \prod_{r \in [T]_0 \setminus S} (t - r).\]
Property~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-phd-ref} follows from the following well-known combinatorial identity.
\begin{fact}[e.g., \cite{concrete} Equation (5.23) or \cite{osnewbounds}] \label{fact:combinatorial}
Let $T \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $p$ be a polynomial of degree less than $T$. Then
\[\sum_{t = 0}^T (-1)^t \binom{T}{t} p(t) = 0.\]
\end{fact}

Expanding out the binomial coefficient in the definition of $\omega$ reveals that
\[|\omega(t)| = \begin{cases}
 \prod\limits_{r \in S \setminus \{t\}} \frac{1}{|t - r|} & \text{ for } t \in S, \\
0 & \text{ otherwise.}
\end{cases}\]

We now use this characterization to establish the improved tail decay property \eqref{eqn:or-sym-decay-ref}. This clearly holds for $t = 1$ with $c_2 = 1/10$, since $|\omega(1)| \le \|\omega\|_1$ and
\[\frac{170}{\delta} \exp(-c_2\sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T}) \ge 340 \cdot e^{-\sqrt{2} / 10} > 1.\]

For $t = c$, we have
\begin{align} \label{eqn:omega-2}
\frac{|\omega(c)|}{\omega(0)} &= \frac{c\prod_{i = 1}^m (2ci^2)}{c(c-1)\prod_{i = 1}^m (2ci^2 - c)} \nonumber \\
&= \frac{1}{c-1}\left(\prod_{i = 1}^m \frac{i^2 - 1/2}{i^2}\right)^{-1} \nonumber \\
&\le \frac{1}{c-1} \left(1 - \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{1}{2i^2}\right)^{-1} \nonumber \\
&\le \frac{1}{c-1} \left(1 - \frac{\pi^2}{12}\right)^{-1} \le \frac{6}{c - 1}
\end{align}
where the first inequality follows from the fact that $\prod_{i = 1}^m (1 - a_i) \ge 1 - \sum_{i = 1}^m a_i$ for $a_i \in (0, 1)$. Now note that
\begin{align*}
\frac{|\omega(c)|}{\|\omega\|_1} &\le \frac{|\omega(c)|}{\omega(0)} \\
&\le \frac{6}{c - 1} \\
&\le \frac{60}{\delta \cdot c^2} & \text{ since } 10/\delta \ge c^2 / (c-1) \\
& \le \frac{170}{\delta \cdot c^2} \cdot e^{-c\sqrt{\delta}/10\sqrt{T}},
\end{align*}
since $\delta \ge 1/T$ and hence $e^{-c\sqrt{\delta}/10\sqrt{T}} \ge e^{-1}$. Thus~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-decay-ref} holds for $t = c$, recalling that $c_2 = 1/10$.

For $t = 2cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we get
\begin{align*}
\frac{|\omega(t)|}{\omega(0)} &= \frac{c\prod_{i = 1}^m (2ci^2)}{(2cj^2 - 1)(2cj^2-c)\prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} |2ci^2 - 2cj^2|} \\
&= \frac{c(m!)^2}{(4c^2j^4 - (2c^2 + 2c)j^2 + c)\prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} (i+j)|i-j|} \\
&= \frac{c}{4c^2j^4 - (2c^2 + 2c)j^2 + c} \cdot \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!}.
\end{align*}
For $j \ge 1$, the first factor is bounded by
\[\frac{c}{4c^2j^4 - (2c^2 + 2c)j^2 + c} \le \frac{3c}{(2cj^2)^2},\]
using the fact that $c \ge 2$. We control the second factor by
\begin{align*}
\frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!} &= \frac{m}{m+j} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m+j-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{m-j+1}{m+1} \\
&\le \left(\frac{m}{m+j} \right)^j \\
&\le  \left(1 - \frac{j}{2m} \right)^j \\
&\le e^{-j^2/2m},
\end{align*}
where the last inequality uses the fact that $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for all $x$.
Since
\[\frac{|\omega(t)|}{\|\omega\|_1} \le \frac{|\omega(2cj^2)|}{\omega(0)} \le \frac{3c}{(2cj^2)^2} \cdot e^{-2cj^2/(4cm)} \le \frac{170}{\delta \cdot t^2} \cdot e^{-t \sqrt{\delta} / 10 \sqrt{T}},\]
this establishes~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-decay-ref}.


What remains is to perform the correlation calculation to establish~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-corr-ref}. For $t = 1$, we observe
\[\frac{|\omega(1)|}{\omega(0)} = \frac{c\prod_{i = 1}^m (2ci^2)}{(c-1)\prod_{i = 1}^m (2ci^2 - 1)} \ge \prod_{i=1}^m \frac{i^2}{i^2 - 1/(2c)} \ge 1.\]
Next, we observe that the total contribution of $t > c$ to $\|\omega\|_1/\omega(0)$ is at most
\begin{equation} \label{eqn:omega-tail}
\sum_{t > c} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{\omega(0)} \le \sum_{j=1}^{m} \frac{3c}{(2cj^2)^2} < \sum_{j=1}^\infty \frac{3}{4cj^4} = \frac{\pi^4}{120 c}.
\end{equation}


Next, we calculate
\begin{align}
\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^T \omega(t) &\ge \omega(0) - \omega(1) - \left( \sum_{t = c}^T |\omega(t)|\right) \nonumber \\
&\ge \omega(0) - \omega(1) - \left( \omega(c) +  \omega(0) \cdot \frac{\pi^4}{120c}\right) & \text{by } \eqref{eqn:omega-tail} \nonumber \\
&\ge - \omega(1) + \omega(0) \left(1 - \frac{6}{c-1} - \frac{\pi^4}{120c}\right) & \text{by } \eqref{eqn:omega-2} \nonumber \\
&\ge - \omega(1)  + (1 - \delta)\omega(0) & \text{by our choice of } c \ge 8/\delta. \label{eqn:fudgethis}
\end{align}
On the other hand,
\begin{align}
\|\omega\|_1 &\le \omega(0) - \omega(1) + \omega(2) + \omega(0) \cdot \frac{\pi^4}{120c} & \text{by } \eqref{eqn:omega-tail} \nonumber \\
&\le -\omega(1) + \omega(0) \left(1 + \frac{6}{c - 1} + \frac{\pi^4}{120c} \right) &\text{by } \eqref{eqn:omega-2}\nonumber \\
&\le -\omega(1) + (1 + \delta)\omega(0) & \text{since } c \ge 8/\delta. \label{eqn:fudgethat}
\end{align}
Combining~\eqref{eqn:fudgethis} and~\eqref{eqn:fudgethat}, and using the fact that $-\omega(1) \ge \omega(0)$ shows that
\[\frac{\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^k \omega(t)}{\|\omega\|_1} \ge \frac{-\omega(1) + (1-\delta) \omega(0)}{-\omega(1) + (1+\delta) \omega(0)} \ge \frac{2-\delta}{2 + \delta} \ge 1 - \delta.\]
This establishes~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-corr-ref}, completing the proof.

Let $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:or-dual} with $\delta:=1/20$. Let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:and-or}, and define $\xi = \Phi \star \psi$. Then by \Cref{prop:ls}, $\xi$ satisfies the following properties:

If $k = 1$, then the function defined by $\omega(0) = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\omega(1) = -\frac{1}{2}$ satisfies the conditions of the proposition for $c_1 = c_2 = 1$. In what follows, we treat the complementary case where $k \ge 2$.

Let $E_+ := \{t \colon \omega(t) > 0, t \ge k\}$, and $E_{-} := \{t\colon \omega(t) < 0, t < k\}$. 
By normalizing, it suffices to construct a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that

\begin{align} & \sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{1}{48 N} \cdot \|\omega\|_1  \label{eqn:thr-sym-pos-corr-ref} \\
& \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1  \label{eqn:thr-sym-neg-corr-ref} \\
& \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \nonumber \\
&\deg p < c_1\sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \sum_{t=0}^k \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \label{eqn:thr-sym-phd-ref} \\

Let $c = 2k\lceil N^{1/k}\rceil$, and let $m = \lfloor \sqrt{T/c} \rfloor$. 
Define the set
\[S = \{1, 2, \dots, k\} \cup \{ci^2 : 0 \le i \le m\}.\]
Note that $|S| = \Omega(k^{-1/2}T^{1/2}N^{-1/(2k)})$. Define the polynomial
\[\omega(t) = \frac{(-1)^{t+(T-m)+1}}{T!} \binom{T}{t} \prod_{r \in [T]_0 \setminus S} (t - r).\]

The signs are chosen so that $\omega(k) < 0$.

We now show that~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} holds. For $t = 1, \dots, k$, we have
\[\frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})}{t^2} \ge \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 \sqrt{k})}{k^2} \ge 1\]
as long as $c_2 \le 1/2$ and $k \ge 2$. Since $|\omega(t)| \le \|\omega\|_1$, the bound holds for $t = 1, \dots, k$.


 For $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we expand out the binomial coefficient in the definition of $\omega$ to obtain
\[|\omega(t)| = \begin{cases}
 \prod\limits_{r \in S\setminus \{t\}} \frac{1}{|t - r|} & \text{ for } t \in S, \\
0 & \text{ otherwise.}
\end{cases}\]
For $t \in \{0, 1, \dots, k\}$, we observe that
\begin{equation} \label{eqn:head-bound}
\frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} = \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - k)}{t! \cdot (k - t)! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - t)} \le \binom{k}{t}.
\end{equation}
Meanwhile, for $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we get
\begin{align*}
\frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} &= \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (ci^2 - k)}{\prod_{i = 1}^k(cj^2 - i) \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} |ci^2 - cj^2|} \\
&\le \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m ci^2}{(cj^2 - k)^{k} \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} c(i+j)|i-j|} \\
&= \frac{k!}{j(cj^2 - k)^{k}} \cdot \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!}.
\end{align*}
The first factor is bounded above by
\[\frac{k!}{(c - k)^k j^{2k+1}}.\] 
As long as $c \ge 2k$ and $k \ge 2$,
this expression is at most
\[\frac{k^k}{(c/2)^kj^4} = \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4}.\]

We control the second factor by
\begin{align*}
\frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!} &= \frac{m}{m+j} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m+j-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{m-j+1}{m+1} \\
&\le \left(\frac{m}{m+j} \right)^j \\
&\le  \left(1 - \frac{j}{2m} \right)^j \\
&\le e^{-j^2/2m},
\end{align*}
where the last inequality uses the fact that $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for all $x$. Hence,
\begin{equation} \label{eqn:tail-bound}
\frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m}.
\end{equation}
This immediately yields
\[\frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{\|\omega\|_1} \le \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{(cj^2)^2} \cdot e^{-cj^2/(2cm)},\]
 which establishes~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} for all $t = cj^2 > k$. 
 
 Moreover, by \eqref{eqn:tail-bound}
\begin{equation} \label{eqn:tail-sum}
\sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j = 1}^m \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k} \cdot |\omega(k)| \cdot  \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{1}{j^4} \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N}.
\end{equation}
Hence, since $\omega(k) < 0$,
\[\sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N} \le \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{48N},\]
which gives~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-pos-corr-ref}.

Finally, to establish~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-neg-corr-ref}, we combine ~\eqref{eqn:head-bound} and~\eqref{eqn:tail-sum} to obtain
\begin{equation} \label{eqn:mass-on-k}
\frac{\|\omega\|_1}{|\omega(k)|} \le \sum_{t = 0}^k \binom{k}{t} + \frac{1}{48 N} < 2^k + 1 < \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4^k.
\end{equation}
We calculate
\begin{align*}
\frac{\|\omega\|_1}{2} - \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| &=  \sum_{t : \omega(t) < 0} (-\omega(t)) - \sum_{t \in E_-} (-\omega(t)) & \text{since $\langle \omega, \mathbf{1} \rangle = 0$}\\
&= \sum_{t \colon \omega(t) < 0, t \geq k} (-\omega(t)) \\
&\ge -\omega(k).
\end{align*}
Rearranging and applying the bound~\eqref{eqn:mass-on-k},
\[\sum_{t \in E_{-}} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{\omega(k)}{\|\omega\|_1}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - 2 \cdot 4^{-k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1.\]
 
Let $\varphi: \{-1, 1\}^M \rightarrow \{-1, 1\}$ be defined such that $\varphi(\mathbf{1})=1/2$, $\varphi(-\mathbf{1})=-1/2$, and $\varphi(x)=0$ for all other $x$. 
Notice that 
\begin{equation}  \sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in \{-1, 1\}^M} \varphi(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) = 0 \label{eq:balanced} \end{equation}
so $\Psi$ has pure high degree $1$, and that $\|\Psi\|_1 = 1$. 


We now prove that (\Cref{eqn:error-amp-pos}) holds. Let $\lambda$ be the distribution on $\{-1, 1\}^{m}$ given by $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$, and let $\lambda^{\otimes M}$ be the product distribution on $(\{-1, 1\}^m)^M$ given by $\lambda^{\otimes M}(x_1, \dots, x_M) = \prod_{i=1}^M |\psi(x_i)|$.
Since $\psi$ is orthogonal to the constant polynomial, it has expected value 0, and hence the string $(\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots)$ is distributed uniformly in $\{-1, 1\}^{M}$
when one samples $(x_1, \dots, x_{M})$ according to $\lambda^{\otimes M}$. This allows us to write
\begin{align}
&\hspace{-2em}\sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in E^+(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M)| \nonumber \\
&\hspace{-2em}= 2^{M} \mathbf{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\varphi( \dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) \cdot \mathbb{I} (\varphi( \dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) > 0 \land \mathsf{ OR}_M\left( \dots, f(x_i), \dots\right) = -1)] \nonumber\\
&\hspace{-2em}= \sum_{z : \varphi(z) > 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, f(x_i), \dots) = -1 | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z]. \label{eqn:error-amp-middle}
\end{align}
Observe that for any bit $b$,
\[\Pr_{x \sim \lambda} [f(x) \ne \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x)) | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x)) = b] = 2\sum_{x \in A_b} |\psi(x)|,\]
where for brevity, we have written $A_{+1} = E_+(\psi, f)$ and $A_{-1} = E_-(\psi, f)$. Therefore, as noted in \cite{sherstovhalfspaces1}, for any given $z \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$, the following two random variables are identically distributed:

\begin{itemize}
\item The string $(\dots, f(x_i), \dots)$, when one chooses $(\dots, x_i, \dots)$ from $\lambda^{\otimes M}$ conditioned on \newline $(\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z$
\item The string $(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots)$, where $y \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently
takes on value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$.
\end{itemize}
Thus, Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-middle} equals
\begin{equation}\sum_{z : \varphi(z) > 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots) = -1], \label{eqn:error-amp-middle2}\end{equation}
where $y \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently
takes on value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. The only term in this sum corresponds to $z=\mathbf{1}$, which we now argue is at most $M \delta^+$.
By \eqref{eqn:error-base-pos}, each $y_i = -1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{1}} |\psi(x)| = 2\sum_{x \in E^+(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le 2\delta^+$.  Hence, for $z = \mathbf{1}$, we have 
\[\Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1] \le 2 M \delta^+\]
by a union bound. Thus Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-middle2} is at most $M \delta^+$, proving \eqref{eqn:error-amp-pos}.

It now remains to prove the bound~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-neg}. By an identical argument as above, we have
\begin{equation}\sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in E^-(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M)| = \sum_{z : \varphi(z) < 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots) = 1]. \label{eqn:error-amp-end}\end{equation}
The only term in the sum corresponds to $z=-\mathbf{1}$, which we argue takes value $\frac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^{M}$. 
Here, each $y_i=-1$ independently with probability $\sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 2\sum_{x \in E^-(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le 2\delta^-$, and $\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, -y_i, \dots)=1$ only if $y_i = -1$ for every $i$. Hence, we conclude that
\[\Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_{M}\left(\dots, -y_i, \dots\right) = 1]  \le (2\delta^-)^M. \]
It follows that Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-end} is at most $\frac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^M$, establishing~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-pos}. This completes the proof.


\Cref{andornor} shows that the function $\mathsf{ OR}_M$ has $(9/10)$-approximate degree $\Omega(\sqrt{M})$. Hence, \Cref{prop:duality} guarantees the existence of a function $\rho : \{-1,1\}^M \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|\rho\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $\Omega(\sqrt{M})$ such that
\begin{equation}
\langle \rho, \mathsf{ OR}_M \rangle \ge \frac{9}{10}.
\end{equation}
What remains is to establish the correlation bound~\eqref{eqn:deg-amp-corr}. Letting $\lambda$ denote the distribution $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$ as in the proof of \Cref{prop:error-amp}, we may write
\begin{align}
& \sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in (\{-1,1\}^m)^M} (\varphi \star \psi) (x_1, \dots, x_M) \cdot \mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, f(x_i), \dots) \nonumber \\
&\qquad= 2^{M} \mathbf{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\varphi( \dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) \cdot \mathsf{ OR}_M\left( \dots, f(x_i), \dots\right)] \nonumber\\
&\qquad= \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^M} \varphi(z) \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, f(x_i), \dots) | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z] \nonumber\\
&\qquad = \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^M} \varphi(z) \cdot \mathbf{E}_{y} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)], \label{eqn:deg-amp-middle}
\end{align}
where $y \in \{-1,1\}^M$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes the value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. (Here, we are using the abbreviated notation $A_{+1} = E_+(\psi, f)$ and $A_{-1} = E_-(\psi, f)$.) We first consider the contribution of the term corresponding to $z = \mathbf{1}$ to the sum. Here, by a union bound,
\begin{align*}
\mathbf{E}_{y} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)] &= 1 - 2 \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1] \\
&\ge 1 - 2 M \cdot \left(2 \sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x)|\right) \\
&\ge 1 - 4 M\delta^+.
\end{align*}
Hence, the term $z = \mathbf{1}$ contributes $\varphi(\mathbf{1}) \cdot (1 - 4 M \delta^+)$ to the sum.

Now we consider the contribution of any term corresponding to $z \ne \mathbf{1}$. Given such a $z$, let $i^*$ be an index such that $z_{i^*} = -1$. Then we have
\begin{align*}
-\mathbf{E}_{y} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)] &= 1 - 2 \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots) = 1] \\
&\ge 1 - 2 \cdot \Pr_{y_{i^*}}[y_{i^*} = -1] \\
&= 1 - 2 \cdot \left(2 \sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)|\right) \\
&\ge 1 - 4 \delta^-.
\end{align*}

We can now lower bound~\eqref{eqn:deg-amp-middle} by
\begin{align*}\hspace{-1.1em}
\varphi(\mathbf{1}) \cdot (1 - 4 M \delta^+) - \sum_{z \ne \mathbf{1}} \varphi(z) (1 - 4\delta^-) &\ge \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^M} \varphi(z) \mathsf{ OR}_M(z) - 4M\delta^+ |\varphi(\mathbf{1})| - 4\delta^- \sum_{z \ne 1} |\varphi(z)| \\
&\ge \frac{9}{10} - 4M\delta^+ - 4\delta^-.\qedhere
\end{align*}

Using the construction of \Cref{prop:error-amp} with $m = N$, $M = 4^k$, and $f = \mathsf{THR}_N^k$, we first obtain a function $\varphi : \{-1,1\}^{4^k} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|\varphi\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $1$ such that
\begin{align*}
&\sum_{x \in E_+(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x)| \le \frac{4^k}{48 N} \\
&\sum_{x \in E_-(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x)| \le \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 4 \cdot 4^{-k} \right)^{4^k} \le \frac{e^{-4}}{2}.
\end{align*}
Now by the construction of \Cref{prop:degree-amp} with $m = 4^k \cdot N$, $M = R/4^{k}$ and $f = \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k$, there exists a function $\rho : \{-1,1\}^{R / 4^k} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|\rho\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $\Omega(2^{-k}\sqrt{R})$ such that
\[ \langle \rho \star (\varphi \star \psi), \mathsf{ OR}_{R/4^k} \circ (\mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N) \rangle \ge \frac{9}{10} - \frac{4R}{48 N} - 2e^{-4} \ge \frac{2}{3}.\]
Let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \mathbb{R}$ be the dual block composition $\rho \star \varphi$. Since the dual block composition preserves $\ell_1$-norms (\Cref{prop:ls}, Condition~\eqref{eqn:ls-norm}) and multiplies pure high degrees (\Cref{prop:ls}, Condition~\eqref{eqn:ls-phd}), the function $\Phi$ itself has $\ell_1$-norm $1$ and pure high degree $\Omega(2^{-k} \sqrt{R})$. The claim now follows from the associativity of dual block composition (\Cref{prop:ls}, Condition~\eqref{eqn:ls-assoc}) and the fact that $\mathsf{ OR}_R = \mathsf{ OR}_{R/4^k} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k}$.

We start by fixing choices of several key parameters:
\begin{itemize}
\item $d= \Theta(2^{-k}\sqrt{R})$ is the pure high degree of the dual witness $\Phi$ for $\mathsf{ OR}_R$ in \Cref{prop:dist-prelim},
\item $T =  \lfloor (8k)^{k/2} \sqrt{R}\rfloor$, 
\item $\alpha = (2k)^k$,
\item $N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha} \rceil R = \Theta((2k)^{k/2} R)$,
\item $\hat{D} = c_1 \sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \cdot d =\Theta(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/4}  \cdot R^{3/4 - 1/(2k)})$, where $c_1$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual},
\item $\beta = c_2 / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}} = \Theta(2^{-3k/4} k^{(-k-3)/4} \cdot R^{-1/4 - 1/(2k)})$, where $c_2$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual}.
\end{itemize}

Let $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:thr-dual}. Let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:dist-prelim}, and define $\xi = \Phi \star \psi$. Then by \Cref{prop:ls}, $\xi$ satisfies the following properties:
\begin{align}& \langle \xi, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle > 2/3, \\
& \| \xi \|_1 = 1, \\ 
& \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \hat{D}, \text{ we have }\langle \xi, p \rangle = 0. 
\end{align}
Recall that $\psi$ was obtained by symmetrizing the function $\omega$ constructed in \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual}.
\Cref{prop:btzeroing} guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tilde{\Omega}(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/4} \cdot R^{3/4 - 1/(2k)})$, the function $\xi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that
\begin{align*}
&\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\
&\langle \zeta, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle \ge \langle \xi, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle - \|\zeta - \xi\|_1 \ge 2/3 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\
&\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\
& \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. 
\end{align*}
Observing that
\[D =  \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\} = \tilde{\Omega}(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/ 4} \cdot R^{3/4-1/(2k)})\]
shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{prop:dist-dual}.

We construct a dual polynomial to witness the lower bound in \Cref{sethm}.

Define the parameters
\begin{itemize}
\item  $\delta = \gamma/4$, 
\item $\alpha = 170/\delta$, 
\item $T=N=\lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha} \rceil R \leq 310 \cdot \gamma^{-1/2} \cdot R$,
\item $\beta = c_2 \cdot \sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T}$, where $c_2$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}.
\end{itemize}

Let 
$\psi$ be the dual witness for $\mathsf{ OR}_N$ from \Cref{prop:or-dual} with $T=N$. Define $\Phi \colon \{-1,1\}^R \to \mathbb{R}$ as follows:
$$\Phi(x) = \begin{cases}
-1/2 & \text{ if } x=(-1, -1, \dots, -1)\\
1/2 & \text{ if } x = (1, 1, \dots, 1)\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}$$

The dual block composition $\Phi \star \psi$ is the same dual witness for $\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ which Bun and Thaler \cite{bt14} used to show that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ
\mathsf{ OR}_N) = \Omega(N^{1/2})$ for $\varepsilon = 1-2^{-R}$. This dual witness was also
used in subsequent works \cite{sherstov14, bchtv}. Curiously, we are
interested in this dual witness for a completely different reason than these
prior works. These prior works were interested in $\Phi \star \psi$ because its correlation
with the target function $\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ is exponentially closer to 1
than is the correlation of $\psi$ with $\mathsf{ OR}_N$. For our purposes,
it will not be essential to exploit such a strong correlation guarantee---rather, we are
interested in $\Phi \star \psi$ because most its ``$\ell_1$-mass''
lies on inputs either with full image or tiny image (i.e.,
most of its mass lies in the domain of $\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$).

As in \Cref{cor:se-reduction}, let $G$ denote the set of all inputs on
which $\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ is defined,
i.e., $$G=\{x_1, \dots, x_R \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \colon (\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_1), \dots, \mathsf{ OR}_N(x_R)) \in
H_{\leq \gamma \cdot R}^R \cup \{\mathbf{-1}\}\}.$$
The analysis in these prior works \cite{bt14,bchtv} implies that 
$\Phi \star \psi$ satisfies the following three properties.
\begin{align} &\|\Phi \star \psi \|_1=1, \label{ughnorm} \\
&\sum_{x \in G}  ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - \sum_{x \in\{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)|
\geq 9/10,  \label{ughcor} \\
&\text{For any polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^{N\cdot R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg p < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \langle \Phi \star \psi, p \rangle = 0,   \label{ughphd}
\end{align}
where $c_1$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-dual}. Indeed, Properties~\eqref{ughnorm} and~\eqref{ughphd} are immediate from \Cref{prop:ls} on the properties of dual block composition. For completeness, we prove that Property~\eqref{ughcor} holds in \Cref{sec:gap-and-corr} below, making use of the fact that $\delta = \gamma/4$ and taking $R$ to be sufficiently large.

\Cref{prop:btzeroing} (with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ set as above) guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$, the function $\Phi \star \psi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that
\begin{align*}
&\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\
&\langle \zeta, \mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle \ge \langle \Phi \star \psi, \mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle - \|\zeta - \Phi \star \psi\|_1 \ge 9/10 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\
&\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\
& \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } D:=\min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. 
\end{align*}
Observing that
\[D =  \min\{c_1\sqrt{\delta T}, \Delta\} = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})\]
shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{sethm} via \Cref{prop:dualitydiedie}.

We begin by observing that the quantity of interest can be written as
\begin{align}
&\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}}  ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - \nonumber \\
&\qquad\qquad \left( \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) + \sum_{x \in\{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \right) \nonumber \\
\ge &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}}  ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - 2 \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)|. \label{eqn:buttz}
\end{align}
We estimate each term of Expression~\eqref{eqn:buttz} separately, beginning with the first term. Just as in the proofs of \Cref{prop:error-amp} and \Cref{prop:degree-amp}, we have
\begin{align*}
\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} (\Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot (\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N)(x) &= \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} \Phi(z) \cdot \mathbb{E}_y[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)]
\end{align*}
where $y \in \{-1,1\}^R$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes the value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. For $z = -\mathbf{1}$, we have by~\eqref{eqn:mybullshitequation} that $2 \sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 0$, so the contribution of the corresponding term to the sum is $1/2$. For $z = \mathbf{1}$, we use the fact that $2 \sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x)| \le \delta$ to compute
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{2} \cdot \mathbb{E}_{y}[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i, \dots)] &= \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 2\Pr_y[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1 ] \right) \\
&\ge \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 2\delta^R\right).
\end{align*}
Hence, the first summand of~\eqref{eqn:buttz} is at least $1-\delta^R$.

We now estimate the second summand, $2 \sum_{x \notin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)|$. As in the proofs of \Cref{prop:error-amp} and \Cref{prop:degree-amp}, we let $\lambda$ denote the distribution with probability mass function $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$. Then
\begin{align*}\hspace{-2.2em}
2\sum_{x \notin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| &= 2^{R+1} \mathbb{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes R}} [|\Phi(\dots, \operatorname{sgn} \psi(x_i), \dots)| \cdot \mathbb{I}(x \notin G)] \\
&= 2\sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} |\Phi(z)| \cdot \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x \notin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z] \\
&= \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x \notin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{-1}] + \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x \notin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{1}].
\end{align*}
We analyze each term of this sum separately. For the first term, observe that by one-sided error of $\psi$, it follows that if $x = (x_1, \dots, x_R)$ is any input $\operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = -1$ for all $i$ then $\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1$ for all $i$. Thus we are guaranteed that $x \in G$, so the contribution of the first summand is zero. To analyze the second summand, let us denote by $r_i \in \{0, 1\}$ the indicator random variable for the event $\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1$ when $x_i$ is drawn from the conditional distribution $(\lambda | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = 1)$. Then
\begin{align*}
\Pr[r_i = 1] &= \Pr_{x_i \sim \lambda}[\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1 | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = 1] \\
&= 2\sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x_i)| \\
&\le \delta
\end{align*}
by~\eqref{eqn:mybullshitequation}. Hence,
\begin{align*}
 \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x \notin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{1}] &\le \Pr\left[ \sum_{i = 1}^R r_i  > \gamma R\right] \\
 &\le \exp\left(-\frac{(\gamma - \delta)R}{3}\right)
\end{align*}
by the multiplicative Chernoff bound.\footnote{The formulation we use here is as follows. Let $r_1, \dots, r_R$ be independent $\{0, 1\}$-valued random variables, $S = \sum_{i=1}^R r_i$, and $\mu = \mathbb{E}[S]$. Then for $\eta > 1$, we have $\Pr[S > (1+\eta) \mu] \le \exp(-\eta \mu / 3)$. In this application, we are taking $\mu \le \delta R$ and $\eta = \gamma R / \mu - 1 > 1$.} Thus, we have
\[2 \sum_{x \notin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \le \exp\left(-\frac{(\gamma - \delta)R}{3}\right).\]
Putting everything together, we see that Expression~\eqref{eqn:buttz} is at least $1 - \delta^R - \exp\left(-(\gamma - \delta) R / 3\right)$ as we wanted to show.

Fix $R >0$, let $c$ be the constant from \Cref{sethm},
$\gamma<(2/3c)^2$ be a sufficiently small constant, and $N= c \cdot \gamma^{-1/2} \cdot R$. As inputs in $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ are interpreted as
elements of $[R]_0^N$, we can equivalently interpret them as elements of $[R+1]^N$,
i.e., as inputs to $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$, for any desired $0 < \gamma_1 < \gamma_2 < 1$.

Set $\gamma_1 = 1-3\gamma/2$ and $\gamma_2=1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$.  
Observe that since $\gamma < (2/3c)^2$, $\gamma_1$ is strictly
greater than $\gamma_2$.

We claim that
\begin{align*} 
&\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(-1) \subseteq \left(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}\right)^{-1}(-1), \text{ and} \\
&\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(+1) \subseteq \left(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}\right)^{-1}(+1).
\end{align*}
Indeed, since inputs in $\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(-1)$ define a probability distribution over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$, with all probabilities being integer multiples of $1/N=\gamma^{1/2}/(cR)$, the statistical distance between any such distribution and
the uniform distribution is at most $1-R/N = 1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$. This follows from the following calculation. 
Amongst probability distributions $(p_1, \dots, p_{R+1})$ over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$ and all probabilities $p_i$ being integer multiples of $1/N$,
it is not hard to see that one maximizes the statistical distance from the uniform distribution over $[R+1]$ by setting $p_1=1-\frac{R-1}{N}$, $p_2=p_3 = \dots = p_{R}=1/N$, and $p_{R+1}=0$. 
The statistical distance from uniform is: 
\begin{align*} 
\frac{1}{2} \left( \left(1-\frac{R-1}{N}-\frac{1}{R+1}\right) + \left(R-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R+1} - \frac1N\right) + \frac{1}{R+1} \right)\\
= 1-\frac{R}{N} + \frac1N - \frac{1}{R+1} \leq 1-\frac{R}{N},
\end{align*}
where we have assumed that $N \geq R+1$, which is true for sufficiently small choice of $\gamma$.

Similarly, since inputs in $\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(1)$ define a probability distribution over $[R+1]$ with support size at most $\gamma \cdot R +1$, 
the statistical distance between any such distribution and
the uniform distribution is at least 
$1-3\gamma/2$. To see
this, let $p=(p_1, \dots, p_{R+1})$ be any distribution of support size at most $\gamma \cdot R$, and let $S = \{i \colon p_i=0\}$ and $\bar{S}$ be the complement of $S$.
Then the statistical distance of $p$ from uniform is at least 
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{2} \left(\sum_{i \in S} \left(p_i - \frac{1}{R+1} \right) \right) + 
\frac{1}{2} \left(\sum_{i \in \bar{S}} \left( p_i - \frac{1}{R+1} \right) \right) 
=
\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{|S|}{R+1} + \left(\sum_{i \in \bar{S}} p_i\right) - \frac{|\bar{S}|}{R+1}\right)\\
= \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{|S|}{R+1} + 1 - \frac{|\bar{S}|}{R+1}\right)
\geq  \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{(1-\gamma) R}{R+1} + 1 - \frac{\gamma R + 1}{R+1}\right)
=  \frac{1}{2} \left(1 +  \frac{R-2\gamma R - 1}{R+1}\right)\\
= 1 - \frac{\gamma R + 1}{R+1} = 1 - \gamma - \frac{\gamma + 1}{R+1} \geq 1-3\gamma/2.
\end{align*}
