\label{rem:TCconnectivity}
Let $X \in \mathrm{CycSp}_{ \geq 0}$ be $p$-complete. 
Using the functorial fiber sequence of Proposition~\ref{functorialfibseq}, we
can give an independent proof 
of Lemma~\ref{connectivity} (and thus of Corollary~\ref{geometricreal}) which is independent of the classical approach to
$\mathrm{TC}$ (i.e., based entirely on the formula \eqref{keyformula}). 
Namely, we argue that $\mathrm{TC}(X) \in \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq -1}$. 

First, suppose that $X$ is an $H \mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}$-module. In this
case, we find that $\mathrm{TC}(X) \in \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq -1}$ thanks to
Proposition~\ref{functorialfibseq}. More generally, if $X$ is a
$p$-complete $H \mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{triv}}$-module, then we find that $X/p$ is an
$H\mathbb{F}_p^{\mathrm{triv}}$-module so that $\mathrm{TC}(X/p) \simeq \mathrm{TC}(X)/p$ belongs
to $\mathrm{Sp}_{\geq -1}$; by $p$-completeness we deduce that $\mathrm{TC}(X) \in \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq
-1}$. 


In general, let $X \in \mathrm{CycSp}_{\geq 0}$ be an arbitrary $p$-complete object. 
Then, we consider the Adams tower for $X$ with respect to the commutative
algebra object $H\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{triv}} \in \mathrm{CycSp}$, i.e., the tower for
the totalization of the cosimplicial object $X \otimes
(H\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{triv}})^{\otimes \bullet + 1}$ (cf.~\cite[Sec.~2.1]{MNN17} for a reference in this generality). 
That is, we consider the tower $\left\{X_n\right\} \in \mathrm{CycSp}$ defined
inductively such that
$X_0 = X$ and $X_{n+1}$ is the fiber of the map $X_{n} \to X_n \otimes
H\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{triv}}$. 
One sees easily that $X_n \in \mathrm{CycSp}_{\geq n}$, and that $X_n$ is $p$-complete since $\pi_i(S^0)$ is finite for $i>0$.

Since $X_{n}/X_{n+1}$ is a $H\mathbb{Z}^{\mathrm{triv}}$-module, it follows from
the previous analysis that $\mathrm{TC}(X_n/X_{n+1}) \in \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq (n-1)}$ for each $n$. 
Inductively, 
it follows now that $\mathrm{TC}(X/X_{n+1}) = \mathrm{TC}(X_0/X_{n+1}) \in \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq -1}$ for
each $n$ and that the maps $\mathrm{TC}(X/X_{n+1}) \to \mathrm{TC}(X/X_{n})$ are surjective
on $\pi_{-1}$. 
Since $X \to X/X_{n+1}$ is an equivalence in degrees $\leq n$, it follows (as in \cite[Lem.~I.2.6]{nikolaus-scholze}) that
\[ X^{hS^1} \simeq \varprojlim (X/X_n )^{hS^1}, \quad 
X^{tS^1} \simeq \varprojlim (X/X_n)^{tS^1}
\]
and therefore by \eqref{keyformula}
\[ \mathrm{TC}(X) \simeq \varprojlim \mathrm{TC}(X/X_n).  \]
Using the Milnor exact sequence 
and the connectivity properties of $\mathrm{TC}(X/X_{n+1})$, 
one concludes that $\mathrm{TC}(X) \in \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq -1}$.

Stated more formally, the preceding discussion shows that the inclusion $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,loc}}_R \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ is the right adjoint of a
\emph{localization} functor on the category $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$. Specifically, $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,loc}}_R$
consists of those objects in $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ which are orthogonal \cite[Sec.
5.4]{Borceux1} to the map
$R[x]^+ \to R[x]^+_{1 + (x)}$, in the sense that such that any map $R[x]^+ \to I$ extends
uniquely over $R[x]^+_{1 + (x)}$.  Moreover, one sees easily from the
construction of the  localization \eqref{loccons} that it is independent of the ground ring $R$.

Analogous statements will be true when we restrict further to the subcategory of henselian nonunital rings; see the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma_nuh}.

We note that if $I$ is a henselian nonunital $R$-algebra then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Considering the equation $x + xy + y = 0$ for $y \in I$, we find that $I$
is local, i.e., $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,loc}}_R$.
\item The root of the equation \eqref{henseq} is necessarily unique: denoting
the equation by $f(x)=0$ for simplicity, if $\alpha,
\alpha' \in I$ are both roots then we have $f'(\alpha) \in 1 + I$ and  
so the Taylor expansion shows that 
$$0 = f(\alpha) - f(\alpha')   \in  \alpha - \alpha' + I(\alpha - \alpha'),$$ whence 
$\alpha = \alpha'$ since $I$ is local.
\end{enumerate}

\label{remark_Lawvere}
The categories $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$, $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,loc}}_R$ and $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ are all examples of models for a {\em
Lawvere} or {\em algebraic theory} \cite[Ch.~3]{ARloc} \cite[Ch.~3]{Borceux}.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category satisfying the following conditions: 


\begin{itemize}
\item[(Law)] $\mathcal C$ has all limits and colimits, and is equipped with a
functor $U \colon \mathcal C\to \mathrm{Sets}$ which is conservative, preserves
sifted colimits, and admits a left adjoint $F \colon \mathrm{Sets}\to\mathcal C$.
\end{itemize}
For example, $\mathcal C$ might be the category of rings, nonunital rings,
groups, etc.  In this case, one takes for $U$ the forgetful functor taking the
underlying set, and its right adjoint $F$ is the free ring, nonunital ring,
group, etc.~on the given set. Denoting by $\{1\}$ a one-point set, the element
$F(\{1\})$ is therefore both compact projective (i.e.,
$\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(F(\{1\}), \cdot)$ commutes with sifted colimits) and a
strong generator (i.e., $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(F(\{1\}), \cdot)$ is faithful and
conservative). The {\em free object of $\mathcal C$ on $n$ generators} is by
definition $\bigsqcup_nF(\{1\})\simeq F(\{1,\dots,n\})$. By the monadicity
theorem, $\mathcal{C}$ is monadic over $\mathrm{Sets}$, via a monad that
preserves sifted colimits. 

Let $\mathcal C'\subset \mathcal C$ be a full subcategory, and assume that
$\mathcal C'$ is closed under limits and sifted colimits (in $\mathcal C$) and that the inclusion $\mathcal C'\subset\mathcal C$ is a right adjoint. Then clearly $\mathcal C'$ also satisfies conditions (Law), with $U'$ given by the restriction of $U$ to $\mathcal C'$. Moreover, the free objects of $\mathcal C'$ are given by applying the left adjoint $\mathcal C\to \mathcal C'$ to the free objects of $\mathcal C$. In practice, this is 
how the ``free objects'' in the above categories are constructed. 

According to general results of Lawvere theory \cite[Thm.~3.9.1]{Borceux} (in fact, we do not use the
results in this paragraph, but the point of view may be helpful), the full
subcategory  $\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma} \subset \mathcal{C}$ of compact projective objects of
$\mathcal{C}$ is the idempotent completion of the full subcategory consisting of
the free objects $\left\{\bigsqcup_{n} F(\{1\}) : n \geq 0\right\}$. Furthermore, $\mathcal{C}$ can be identified with the category of presheaves on $\mathcal{C}_\Sigma$ which commute with finite products. In particular, objects of $\mathcal{C}$ can be identified with sets equipped with various ``operations'' arising from maps between the free objects satisfying various relations.

universal homotopies" from \cite{Suslinlocal}, which has been crucial to many of the known
rigidity results in $K$-theory.

\label{rem:fpcaseeasier}
While the 
the full strength of pseudocoherence appears to be necessary to obtain results

follows from Proposition~\ref{rigidity:henspaircharp} and the observation that

continuity statement of \cite{GHlocal} (and a similar filtered colimit
argument). Thus, for $\mathbb{Z}_p$-algebras at least, one can prove the main

Theorem~\ref{mainthm} is false integrally; that is, the integral

As an example,

residue field $\mathbb{F}_p$. 
Then $\mathrm{TC}(R), \mathrm{TC}(\mathbb{F}_p)$ are $p$-complete spectra, so

However, $K_1(R, \mathfrak{m}) =\mathrm{ker}(R^{\times} \to
\mathbb{F}_p^{\times})$ which will essentially never be derived $p$-complete. 
For instance, consider the power series ring $R_0 =  \mathbb{F}_p[[x]]$ and let
$R = (R_0)_{\mathrm{perf}}$ be the perfection of $R_0$. 
We have a surjection $R \to \mathbb{F}_p$, whose kernel is the henselian ideal
$I = \bigcup (x^{1/p^n})$. 
In this case, $\mathrm{ker}(R^{\times} \to \mathbb{F}_p^{\times})$ is a
nonzero
$\mathbb{Z}[1/p]$-module, which in particular is not derived $p$-complete.

\label{henspairequivtocontinuity}
One can see that Theorem~\ref{Kcont} is in fact equivalent to Theorem~\ref{mainthm} (our main theorem on henselian pairs).  Indeed, suppose Theorem~\ref{Kcont} is known, and let $(R,I)$ be a henselian pair.  We want to show that $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R)/p\rightarrow K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)/p$ is an equivalence.  Since $K$ and $\mathrm{TC}/p$ commute with filtered colimits, so does $K^{\mathrm{inv}}/p$, hence we can assume $(R,I)$ is the henselization of a finite type $\mathbb{Z}$-algebra at an ideal.  

Let $\widehat{R}$ denote the $I$-adic completion of $R$. 
By N\'eron--Popescu desingularization \cite{Popescu1, Popescu2} (see also
\cite[Tag 07BW]{stacks-project}), applicable in view of the geometric regularity of $R \to
\widehat{R}$ (see \cite[7.8.3(v)]{EGA_IV_2}), the map $R\rightarrow \widehat{R}$ is
ind-smooth, i.e., we can write $\widehat{R}$ as a filtered colimit of smooth
$R$-algebras.
Given a smooth $R$-algebra $A$ and a map $A \to \widehat{R}$ of
$R$-algebras, it follows
that the map $R \to A$ admits a section by Elkik's theorem
(Theorem~\ref{elkikthm}). 
Therefore,  we deduce that $R\rightarrow \widehat{R}$ is a filtered colimit
of split injections.  Thus the claim for $(R,I)$ (i.e., that $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R)/p \to
K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)/p$ is an equivalence) will follow from the claim for
$(\widehat{R}, I \widehat{R})$.  (This is a standard Artin approximation argument.)

However, by the above continuity in $K$ and $\mathrm{TC}$, we have
$$K^{\mathrm{inv}}(\widehat{R})/p\overset{\simeq}{\rightarrow}\varprojlim
K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I^n)/p.$$  On the other hand, the right hand side is a constant limit
with value $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)/p$, by Theorem~\ref{DGMthm}.  This gives the claim for
$(\widehat{R}, I\widehat{R})$, and therefore in general, by the above argument.

Without assuming $\mathbb{Z}$-linear structure, one can get similar results by
replacing $-\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}/p^i\mathbb{Z}$ with $-\otimes S_i$ for
any reasonable tower of $E_\infty$-algebras $\left\{S_i\right\}$ of which $p$-adically approximates the sphere spectrum, for example the tower coming from the usual cosimplicial Adams resolution associated to $S^0\rightarrow H\mathbb{F}_p$.

In this paper, we will use the language of $\infty$-categories
and higher algebra
\cite{HTT, HA}. On the one hand, the constructions of algebraic $K$-theory and of
the cyclotomic trace are of course much older than the theory of $\infty$-categories. Many of
our arguments use standard homotopical techniques that could be carried out
in a modern model category of spectra, and we  have tried to minimize the use of
newer technology in the exposition when possible. On the other hand, we rely crucially
on the Nikolaus--Scholze \cite{nikolaus-scholze} approach to cyclotomic spectra,
which is $\infty$-categorical in nature.

We let $K$ denote connective $K$-theory and $\mathbb{K}$ denote its
nonconnective analog; $\mathrm{TC}$ denotes topological cyclic homology. 
Given a ring $R$ and an ideal $I \subset R$, we let $K(R, I)$
(resp.~$\mathbb{K}(R, I)$) denote the relative $K$-theory (resp.~relative nonconnective
$K$-theory), defined  as $\mathrm{fib}(K(R) \to K(R/I))$ and
$\mathrm{fib}(\mathbb{K}(R) \to \mathbb{K}(R/I))$. We define $ K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R, I), \mathrm{TC}(R, I)$
similarly. Finally, following traditional practice in algebraic $K$-theory, we
will sometimes write $K_*(R; \mathbb{Z}/p^r \mathbb{Z})$ for the mod $p^r$
homotopy of the spectrum $K(R)$ (i.e., $\pi_*( K(R)/p^r)$) and similarly for
$\mathrm{TC}$.

Given a ring $R$, we can form both its Hochschild homology $\mathrm{HH}(R/\mathbb{Z})$
and its topological Hochschild homology spectrum $\mathrm{THH}(R)$.  The main structure on Hochschild homology is the circle action,
enabling one to form the \emph{negative cyclic homology} $\mathrm{HC}^-(R/\mathbb{Z}) =
\mathrm{HH}(R/\mathbb{Z})^{hS^1}$. However,
there is additional information contained in topological Hochschild homology, encoded in the structure of a \emph{cyclotomic spectrum}.
Formally, cyclotomic spectra form a symmetric monoidal, stable $\infty$-category $(\mathrm{CycSp},
\otimes, \mathbf{1})$, and $\mathrm{THH}(R) \in \mathrm{CycSp}$.  
An object of $\mathrm{CycSp}$ is in particular a spectrum with a circle action but also
further information. 
This structure enables one to form the topological cyclic homology $\mathrm{TC}(R) =
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{CycSp}}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{THH}(R))$. 
Introduced originally by B\"okstedt--Hsiang--Madsen \cite{BHM}, nowadays there are
several treatments 
of $\mathrm{CycSp}$ by various
authors, including Blumberg--Mandell \cite{BMcyc},
Barwick--Glasman \cite{BG}, Nikolaus--Scholze \cite{nikolaus-scholze}, and  Ayala--Mazel-Gee--Rozenblyum
\cite{ayala-mg-rozenblyum}. 
In particular, the paper \cite{nikolaus-scholze} shows that the structure of $\mathrm{CycSp}$
 admits a dramatic simplification in the bounded-below case.

The purpose of this section is to prove a structural property of $\mathrm{TC}$. 
The datum of a circle action is essentially infinitary in nature: for example,
forming $S^1$-homotopy fixed points is an infinite homotopy limit, and the
construction $R \mapsto \mathrm{HC}^-(R/\mathbb{Z})$ does not
commute with filtered homotopy colimits.
Classical presentations of the homotopy
theory of cyclotomic spectra and $\mathrm{TC}$ usually involve infinitary limits, such
as 
a homotopy limit over a fixed point tower. 
However, in this section, we prove the slightly surprising but fundamental  property that $\mathrm{TC}/p$ commutes with filtered
colimits. Our proof is based on the simplification to the theory
$\mathrm{CycSp}$ in the bounded-below case demonstrated by Nikolaus--Scholze
\cite{nikolaus-scholze}.

The $\infty$-category $\mathrm{CycSp}$ naturally has the structure of a presentably
symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category\footnote{Meaning, a presentable $\infty$-category with symmetric monoidal tensor product commuting with colimits in each variable separately; or in other words a commutative algebra object in $\operatorname{Pr}^L$ with respect to Lurie's tensor product.} and the tensor product recovers the smash
product on the level of underlying spectra with $S^1$-action. Moreover, the
forgetful functor $\mathrm{CycSp}\to \mathrm{Sp}$ reflects equivalences, is exact, and preserves
all colimits. These properties may be deduced from the general formalism of lax equalizers; see \cite[II.1]{nikolaus-scholze}.

A basic observation which goes into proving the main result of this section is
that the above formula makes $\mathrm{TC}$ have an additional finiteness property that
theories such that $\mathrm{TC}^-$ and $\mathrm{TP}$ do not enjoy. Roughly speaking the idea is
the following: if in the definition above we were to replace $\mathrm{can}_X-\varphi_X$
with just $\mathrm{can}_X$, then the fiber would be $\Sigma X_{hS^1}$, and this certainly commutes with colimits.  We will see that $\varphi_X$ is close enough to vanishing modulo $p$ to deduce the same conclusion for $\mathrm{TC}(X)/p$.  
As another example of such finiteness phenomena, 
compare for instance \cite{AMN}, where it was shown that the topological
cyclic homology  of a smooth and proper dg category over a finite field 
is a perfect $H \mathbb{Z}_p$-module.

It is the classical approach to topological cyclic homology in which important structures such as the de
Rham-Witt complex appear \cite{Hesselholt}, and in which the sequence \eqref{isotropysep} below plays a fundamental role.  Using the classical approach we also obtain the following lemma.
In Remark~\ref{rem:TCconnectivity} below, we 
will also give  a proof purely based on the Nikolaus--Scholze approach.

A \emph{saturated} Dieudonn\'e complex 
$(X^{\ast}, d, F)$ is a  $p$-torsion-free cochain complex
equipped with an operator $F: X^{\ast} \to X^{\ast}$ such that $dF = pFd$, the
opeartor $F: X^n \to X^n$ is injective, and the image of $F$ consists
precisely of those $x \in X^n$ such that $p $ divides $dx$; this implies that one
can define uniquely an operator $V$ such that $FV = VF = p$.  
A saturated Dieudonn\'e complex $(X^{\ast}, d, F)$ is called \emph{strict} if 
$X^{\ast}$ is in addition complete for the filtration defined by
$\{\mathrm{im}(V^n, d V^n)\}$. The de Rham--Witt complex of an ind-smooth
algebra is a strict Dieudonn\'e complex, and the functor $A \mapsto W
\Omega_A^{\ast}$ commutes with filtered colimits from ind-smooth
$\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras to the category of strict Dieudonn\'e complexes (where
colimits in the latter involve a completion process).

In this section we consider various applications to the continuity problem in algebraic $K$-theory and to the related problem of describing the pro $K$-theory of formal schemes.
In particular we show that, under mild hypotheses, algebraic $K$-theory with finite coefficients is continuous for complete noetherian rings (Theorem~\ref{Kcont}). 
We also show that algebraic $K$-theory satisfies a ``derived'' form of $p$-adic
continuity for rings that are henselian along $p$ (Theorem~\ref{derivedpadiccont}), extending
results of Geisser--Hesselholt \cite{GHlocal}. Finally, we prove a pro version of
the Geisser--Levine \cite{GL} theorem on the $p$-adic $K$-theory of regular local
$\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras to describe (under mild hypotheses) the pro abelian groups 
$\{K_*(A/I^s; \mathbb{Z}/p^r\mathbb{Z})\}_s$ when $A$ is a regular local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra and $I \subset A$ is any ideal, extending results of Morrow \cite{Morrow-HW}.

In order to apply our earlier results to this question, we observe that if $(R, I)$ is a henselian pair  then Theorem~\ref{mainthm} implies that 
the map \eqref{contmap} becomes an equivalence modulo $p$ if and only if the
corresponding map $\mathrm{TC}(R) \to \varprojlim_s \mathrm{TC}(R/I^s)$ becomes an equivalence
modulo $p$. 
This latter question is often more tractable and has been carefully
studied in the recent work of Dundas--Morrow \cite{DundasMorrow}, who show that such
continuity for topological cyclic homology holds quite generally under the assumption of
$F$-finiteness.

Although the previous theorem concerns $p$-adic rings, its proof uses Gabber rigidity for $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]$-algebras, via a clever trick due to Suslin.  Here we will obtain a generalization of Theorem \ref{GHcontinuity} using our version of rigidity, which directly applies to $p$-adic rings.  We observe also that the proof naturally yields something slightly
stronger than an equivalence of pro abelian groups.

In our proof above, we only need to invoke the second half of Gabber's work,
which is also covered by Gillet--Thomason \cite{GT}.

However, our entire line of reasoning is in some sense modeled on the first half
of Gabber's proof. (The exceptions are Proposition \ref{rigidity:henspaircharp},
which is the new characteristic $p$ ingredient, and the commutation of $\mathrm{TC}/p$
with filtered colimits, which is a necessary technical statement.)  So we are
not really avoiding the first half of Gabber's proof, just explicating it in a
modified context.  Let us note in particular that the projective
pseudocoherence of $K$-theory is our replacement for Suslin's ``method of
universal homotopies" from \cite{Suslinlocal}, which has been crucial to many of the known
rigidity results in $K$-theory.

A key source of examples of cyclotomic spectra arises as follows.

As usual, we will write $\mathrm{TC}(R), \mathrm{TC}^-(R), \mathrm{TP}(R)$ in place of $\mathrm{TC}(\mathrm{THH}(R)), \mathrm{TC}^-(\mathrm{THH}(R)), \mathrm{TP}(\mathrm{THH}(R))$.
 
For commutative $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras, Corollary~\ref{TCring} can be deduced
using the description of Hesselholt \cite{Hesselholt} of $\mathrm{THH}$ of smooth
$\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras in terms of the de Rham--Witt complex; we detail this in
subsection~\ref{dRWapproach} below.
 
In the case of square-zero extensions, 
the verification (called the \emph{$p$-limit axiom})  of
Corollary~\ref{TCring} plays an important role in
the proof that relative $K$-theory and $\mathrm{TC}$ with finite coefficients agree for nilimmersions of rings
in McCarthy \cite{mccarthy}. 
 
Let $M$ be an $\mathbb{E}_1$-monoid in the $\infty$-category of spaces, so that
one can form the spherical monoid ring $\Sigma^\infty_+ M$. 
The formula for $\mathrm{TC}$ of spherical 
monoid rings \cite[Lemma IV.3.1]{nikolaus-scholze} (preceded by the formula for
spherical group rings appearing already in \cite[Eq. (0.3)]{BHM})
shows that for any such $R$, 
the cyclotomic structure map $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \mathrm{THH}(R)^{tC_p}$ factors
$S^1$-equivariantly through
$\mathrm{THH}(R)^{hC_p}$, which is called a \emph{Frobenius lift} in
\cite{nikolaus-scholze}. For cyclotomic spectrum $X$ with a Frobenius lift, the construction  of
($p$-complete) $\mathrm{TC}$ simplifies: one has a fiber square 
\cite[Prop. IV-3.4]{nikolaus-scholze} relating $\mathrm{TC}(X)$ to $\Sigma
X_{hS^1}$ and two copies of $X$. It follows from this that the construction  
$M \mapsto \mathrm{TC}( \Sigma^\infty_+ M)/p$ commutes with filtered colimits in $M$. 
Since the free associative algebra is a spherical monoid ring, and since $\mathrm{TC}$
is already known to commute with geometric realizations, one can also deduce
Corollary~\ref{TCring} in this way.

suspension spectrum of the corepresentable associated to $

A projectively pseudocoherent functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$ commutes with filtered

\label{perfex}
Let $R$ be a perfect $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra, i.e., such that the Frobenius is
an isomorphism. Then the map $K(R)/p^r \to \mathrm{TC}(R)/p^r$ is an
equivalence on connective covers for each $r \geq 0$.

|x| = -2.$$

v(x,t)=u_2(x,t):=f_{h}(x,t), & \textrm{on}\,\, \Sigma.
\end{array}
\right.
\end{equation}
We let $ w=v-u_2$. Therefore, $w$ solves the following homogenous boundary value problem
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{lll}
\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}w(x,t)=a(x)\partial_tu_2(x,t)+q(x)u_2(x,t) & \textrm{in}\,\,  Q,\cr
w(x,0)=\partial_tw(x,0)=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, \mathrm{M},\cr
w(x,t)=0, & \textrm{on}\,\,  \Sigma.
\end{array}
\right.
$$
Using the fact that  $a(x)\partial_tu_2+q(x)u_2 \in W^{1,1}(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))$ with $u_2(\cdot,0)=\partial_t u_2(\cdot,0)\equiv 0$, by Lemma \ref{L.1.1}, we deduce that
$$
w\in \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})\cap
H^1_0(\mathrm{M})).
$$
Therefore, we have constructed a special solution
  $$ 
  \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\mathrm{M})) \cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})),
  $$
to the backward wave equation
\begin{align*}
\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta-a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}u_1(x,t)&=0,  \quad (x,t) \in Q, \\
u_1(x,T)=u_1(x,T)&=0,  \quad x \in \mathrm{M},
\end{align*}
having the special form
\begin{equation}\label{4.6}
u_1(x,t)=(\theta_1\psi_{-a_1})( t,x)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_{1,h}(x,t),
\end{equation}
which corresponds to the coefficients $-a_1$ and $q_1$, where
$r_{1,h}$ satisfies for $h<h_0$
\begin{equation}\label{4.7}
h^{-1}\norm{r_{1,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{\partial_t r_{1,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{\nabla
r_{1,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
\end{equation}
Integrating by parts and using Green's formula (\ref{3.4}), we find
\begin{multline}\label{4.8}
\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M}\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}w\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t
= \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tu_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t
=-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \partial_\nu w\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t.
\end{multline}
Taking (\ref{4.8}), (\ref{4.6}) into account, we deduce
\begin{multline}\label{4.9}
-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tu_2\overline{u}_1(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\,\mathrm{d} t 
=\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}}\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2,q_2}} f_{h}(x,t)\overline{g}_h(x,t) \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t
\end{multline}
where $g_h$ is given by
$$
g_h(x,t)=(\theta_1\psi_{-a_1})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h},\quad (x,t)\in \Sigma.
$$
It follows from (\ref{4.9}), (\ref{4.6}) and (\ref{4.3}) that
\begin{multline}\label{4.10}
ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\theta_2 \overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)(\psi_{a_2}\psi_{-a_1})( x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\,\mathrm{d} t =\cr
\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t
-ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(t,x)e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t r_{2,h}(\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1})(x,t) e^{-i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tr_{2,h}(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2(x,t)\overline{u}_1(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt \cr
= \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h \para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t+\mathscr{R}_h.
\end{multline}
In view of (\ref{4.7}) and (\ref{4.4}), we have
\begin{equation}\label{4.11}
\abs{\mathscr{R}_h}\leq C\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, by the trace theorem, we find
\begin{eqnarray}\label{4.12}
\bigg|\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}}\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}(f_{h}) \overline{g}_h \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t \bigg|
&\leq & \norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}} \norm{f_h}_{H^{1}(\Sigma)}\norm{g_h}_{L^2(\Sigma)}\cr
&\leq & Ch^{-3}\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}
-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}.
\end{eqnarray}
The estimate (\ref{4.2}) follows easily from (\ref{4.10}), (\ref{4.11}) and (\ref{4.12}).\\
This completes the proof of the Lemma.

We take two solutions to (\ref{3.11}) of the form
\begin{align*}
\widetilde{\theta}_1(t,r,\xi)&=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi), \\
\widetilde{\theta}_2(t,r,\xi)&=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r).
\end{align*}
Now we change variable in the left term of (\ref{4.1}), $x=\exp_{y}(r\xi)$, $r>0$ and
$\xi\in S_{y}\mathrm{M}_1$, we have
\begin{multline}\label{4.14}
\int_0^T\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\overline{\theta}_1\theta_2)(x,t)\psi_{a}(x,t)  \,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t \cr
=\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)(\overline{\widetilde{\theta}}_1\widetilde{\theta}_2)( t,r,\xi)
\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t,r,\xi)
\alpha^{1/2} \, \mathrm{d} r \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t\cr
=\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)\phi^2( t-r)\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t,r,\xi)\Psi(\xi)  \, \mathrm{d} r \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)
\, \mathrm{d} t\cr
=\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_\mathbb{R} \widetilde{a}( t-\tau,y,\xi)\phi^2(\tau)\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t, t-\tau,\xi)\Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)
\, \mathrm{d} t\cr
=\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_\mathbb{R} \widetilde{a}( t-\tau,y,\xi)\phi^2(\tau)\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ t}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}
\Psi(\xi)  \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)\cr
=2\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\int_0^T \frac{d}{dt}\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ t}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}
\Psi(\xi)  \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)\cr
=2\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ T}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}-1}
\Psi(\xi)  \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi).
\end{multline}
By the support properties of the function $\phi$, we get that the left-hand side term in (\ref{4.14}) reads
\begin{multline*}
  \int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{T}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}-1}
\Psi(\xi)  \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)=\cr
\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(s,y,\xi)ds}-1}
\Psi(\xi) \mu(y,\xi) \, 
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi).
\end{multline*}
Then, by (\ref{4.14}) and (\ref{4.2}) we get
\begin{multline}\label{4.15}
\abs{\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\para{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)}-1}
\Psi(\xi)  \,  
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)}\cr
 \leq C\para{h+h^{-2}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}} \norm{\Psi}_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_{1})}.
\end{multline}
This completes the proof of the Lemma.

Let $(y,\theta)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1$ be a fixed and let $\Psi_\kappa$ be the positive function given by (\ref{4.16}). We extend $\mathcal{I}(a)$ by zero in $\partial_-S\mathrm{M}$, then,  we have
\begin{multline}\label{4.22}
\Big|\exp\para{-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)} -1 \Big|=\Big|
\displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\Big[ \exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big)-1  \Big]\,d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|\cr
\leq\quad \Big| \displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\Big[\exp\Big( -\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big)
-\exp\Big(-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)\Big)   \Big]  \,d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|\cr
 +\Big| \displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1} \Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\Big[\exp\Big(-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)  \Big)-1 \Big]
 d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|.

Therefore, since we have
$$\begin{array}{lll} \Big| \!\exp\Big(
\!-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)\Big)
\!-\!\exp\Big(\! -\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)
\! \Big) \Big|\!\!\!&\leq&\!\!\! C\Big|\displaystyle \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)-\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)\Big|,\cr
\end{array}$$
and using the fact that
$$
\Big|\displaystyle \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)-\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)\Big|\leq C \,|\theta-\xi|,
$$
 we deduce upon applying Lemma \ref{L.4.2} with $\Psi=\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\cdot)$ the following estimation
\begin{multline*}
\Big|\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)\Big)-1
\Big|\leq \cr
C\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\,|\theta-\xi|\,d\omega_y(\xi)+C\Big(

\Big)\|\Psi_{\kappa}\|_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_1)}^{2}.

 On the other hand, by (\ref{4.20}) and (\ref{4.19}), we have the following inequality

 \Big|\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)\Big)-1
\Big|\leq C \,(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}+C\Big(
h^{-2}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+h
\Big)(1-\kappa)^{-(3+n)}.
 $$
 Selecting $(1-\kappa)$ small such that $(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}=h(1-\kappa)^{-(n+3)}$,
that is $(1-\kappa)=h^{2n/1+2n^2+6n}$, we find two constants $\delta>0$ and $\beta>0$
such that
$$\Big| \exp \Big( -\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big)-1 \Big|\leq
C \Big[
h^{-\delta}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+h^{\beta}
\Big].$$
 Now, using the fact that $|X|\leq e^{M}\,|e^{X}-1|$ for any $|X|\leq M$, we
deduce that
$$\Big| -\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big|\leq e^{M_{1}T}\Big| \exp\Big( -\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)  \Big)-1
\Big|.$$ Hence, we conclude that for all $\theta\in S_y\mathrm{M}_1$ and
$y\in $ we have
$$
\Big|\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big|\leq C \Big(h^{-\delta}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+h^{\beta}\Big).
$$ 
The proof of Lemma \ref{L.4.4} is complete.

From the equality (\ref{4.10}) and the expressions (\ref{4.6}) and (\ref{4.3}), it follows  that
\begin{multline}\label{5.3}
\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)\psi_{a}(x,t)\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt = -
\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t
\cr +ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\theta_2 \overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)(\psi_{a_2}\psi_{-a_1})( x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\,\mathrm{d} t +ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t))\overline{r}_{1,h}e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)(\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1})(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t
-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(x,t)e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t r_{2,h}(\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1})(x,t) e^{-i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t
-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tr_{2,h}(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)(\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{-a_1})(x,t)r_{2,h}(x,t)e^{-i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t -\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(x,t)e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr -\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)(r_{2,h}\overline{r}_{1,h})(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t .
\end{multline}
We set 
$$\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)\psi_{a}(x,t)\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt = -\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t +\mathscr{R}'_h.$$
In view of (\ref{4.7}) and (\ref{4.4}), we have
\begin{equation}\label{5.4}
\abs{\mathscr{R}'_h}\leq C\para{h+h^{-1} \|a\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})}}\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, by the trace theorem, we find
\begin{eqnarray}\label{5.5}
\bigg|\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}}\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}(f_{h}) \overline{g}_h \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t \bigg|
&\leq & \norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}} \norm{f_h}_{H^{1}(\Sigma)}\norm{g_h}_{L^2(\Sigma)}\cr
&\leq & Ch^{-3}\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}
-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}.

Furthermore
\begin{multline} \label{5.6}
\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt = \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)(1-\psi_{a}(x,t))\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt \cr + \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)\psi_{a}(x,t)\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt
\end{multline}
and since
$$
\abs{1-\psi_a(x,t)}\leq C\norm{a}_{\mathcal{C}(\mathrm{M})}
$$
we deduce that 
 $$
 \bigg|\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)(1-\psi_{a}(x,t))\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt\bigg| \leq C\norm{a}_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})} \norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.$$ Combining with (\ref{5.4}), (\ref{5.5}) and (\ref{5.6}), the estimate (\ref{5.2}) follows.\\
  This completes the proof of the Lemma.

As in Lemma \ref{L.4.2}, we take two solutions to (\ref{3.11}) of the form

\widetilde{\theta}_1(t,r,\xi)&=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi), \\

We change variable in the left term of (\ref{5.2}), $x=\exp_{y}(r\xi)$, $r>0$ and $\xi\in S_{y}\mathrm{M}_1$. We have

We fix $(y,\theta)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}$ and let the positive function $\Psi_\kappa$ given by (\ref{5.10}),  we have

 On the other hand, by (\ref{4.20}) and (\ref{4.19}), we obtain

 \Big|\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\theta)\Big|\leq C \,(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}+C\Big(

 $$
 Take $(1-\kappa)$ small such that $(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}=h(1-\kappa)^{-(n+3)}$,

C \Big[

The proof of Lemma \ref{L.5.3} is complete.
}

\int_{S\mathrm{M}} \left[ \vert \overset{h}{\nabla} u \vert ^2-\langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle+(n-2) \vert Hu\vert ^2 \right] \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}= -\int_{\partial_+S\mathrm{M}} \langle V,\nu\rangle \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2},

\begin{equation}\label{2.39}
\vert \int_{\partial_+S\mathrm{M}}\langle V,\nu\rangle  \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} \vert \leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})},
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation}\label{2.40}
\vert \int_{S\mathrm{M}} \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle  \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \vert \leq k^+  \int_{S\mathrm{M}}\vert H \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}u\vert^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}.
\end{equation}
Combining (\ref{2.40}), (\ref{2.39}) and (\ref{2.38}) with item (3) of Lemma \ref{L.2.2}, we find 
\begin{equation}\label{2.41}
(1-k^+)\int_{S\mathrm{M}}  \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}+(n-2) \int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert Hu\vert ^2  \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}\leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})}.
\end{equation}
For $k^+<1$ and $n\geq 2$, we deduce the estimate
\begin{equation}\label{2.42}
\int_{S\mathrm{M}}  \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \leq  C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})}.
\end{equation}
In view of the definition of $H$, in (\ref{2.30}), there exists a constant $C$ such that 
$$
\vert Hu \vert^2 \leq C  \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 .
$$ 
Using the item (2) of Lemma \ref{L.2.2} and (\ref{2.30}), we conclude that 
$$
\Vert f \Vert ^2_{L^2(S\mathrm{M})}=\int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert Hu \vert^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}\leq C \int_{S\mathrm{M}}  \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \leq  C\Vert\mathcal{I} f \Vert^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})},
 $$ and the Theorem \ref{theorem} is done. \\   
 Now, we come back to prove (\ref{2.38})-(\ref{2.39}) and (\ref{2.40}). First, we start with (\ref{2.40}). By (\ref{2.8}) we find
 \begin{equation}\label{2.43}
 \vert \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle \vert \leq K^+(x,\xi) \vert \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u(x,\xi) \vert^2,\quad \forall (x,\xi)\in S\mathrm{M}.
 \end{equation}
  Furthermore, the lemma \ref{L.2.3} combined with (\ref{2.43}) gives the following estimate
\begin{align} \label{2.44}
\int_{S \mathrm{M}} \vert \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle \vert \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} & \leq k^+ \int_{S \mathrm{M}}  \vert H\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u \vert^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} & \cr & \leq k^+ \int_{S \mathrm{M}}  \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1},
\end{align} 
This completes the proof of (\ref{2.40}).\\
We prove now (\ref{2.38}).  Since we have $Hu=-f$ and  $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}f=0$, then the Pestov's identity (\ref{2.31}) gives 
 \begin{equation}\label{2.45}
 \vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2+  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\textrm{div}}(V) + \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\textrm{div}}(W)- \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle=0.
 \end{equation}
 Avoiding eventual singularities of $u$  on $T \partial\mathrm{M}$, we will consider the variety $\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ defined by $$\mathrm{M}_{\rho}=\{x \in \mathrm{M},\quad d_\mathrm{g}(x,\partial \mathrm{M}) \geq \rho \},$$ where $\rho >0$. In some neighbourhood of $\partial \mathrm{M},$ the function $x \mapsto d_\mathrm{g}(x,\partial \mathrm{M})$ is smooth and $\partial \mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ is strictly convex for sufficiently small $\rho >0.$ The function $u$ is smooth on $S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ since $S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}\subset S\mathrm{M} \setminus S(\partial \mathrm{M})$. Integrating  (\ref{2.45}) over $S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ and using the formula divergence (\ref{2.27}) and (\ref{2.28}), we find 
 \begin{align*}
 \int_{S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}}\left[ \vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2- \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle\right]\, \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}= &
 -\int_{S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}} \left[ \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\textrm{div}}(V)  + \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\textrm{div}}(W)\right]\, \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \cr =&
  -\int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}} \langle V, \nu \rangle \quad d\sigma^{2n-2} -(n-2)\int_{S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}} \langle W, \xi \rangle \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1},
 \end{align*}
 where $\nu=\nu_{\rho}(x)$ is the unit vector of the outer normal to the boundary of $\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$.
 In view of (\ref{2.33}), we have 
 $$\langle W, \xi \rangle=\langle\xi,\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u\rangle ^2 = \vert Hu\vert ^2.$$
Hence, we obtain the equality 
\begin{equation}\label{2.46}
 \int_{S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}}\left[ \vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2- \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle+(n-2) \vert Hu\vert^2 \right]  \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}= -\int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}} \langle V, \nu \rangle \,d\sigma^{2n-2}.
\end{equation} 
Now, we wish pass to the limit as $\rho \rightarrow 0.$ We will apply the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem.  Denote by $\mathbb{\chi}_\rho$ the characteristic function of the set $S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ and by $p$  the projection $p : \partial S\mathrm{M} \longrightarrow  \partial S\mathrm{M}_\rho$, $p(x,\xi)=(x',\xi'),$ where $x'$ 
 is such that the geodesic $\gamma_{xx'}$ has length $\rho$ and intersects $\partial \mathrm{M}$ orthogonally at $x$ and $x'$, and $\xi'$ is obtained 
 by the parallel translation of the vector $\xi$ along $\gamma_{xx'}$. So the equality (\ref{2.46}) becomes 
 \begin{equation}\label{2.47}
 \int_{S\mathrm{M}}\left[ \vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2- \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle+(n-2) \vert Hu\vert ^2 \right] \mathbb{\chi}_\rho  \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}= -\int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}} \langle V, \nu \rangle p_* ( d\sigma^{2n-2}).
\end{equation} 
Note that all the integrands of (\ref{2.47}) are smooth on $S\mathrm{M} \setminus \partial S \mathrm{M}$ and so, they converge towards their values almost everywhere, when $\rho \rightarrow 0$. 
Since the functions $\vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2$ and $\vert Hu\vert ^2$  are positive and the second function satifies (\ref{2.43}), then the left side of (\ref{2.47}) converges as $\rho \rightarrow 0$.  To apply the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem in (\ref{2.47}), it remains to prove that $\vert \langle V, \nu \rangle p_*  \vert$ is bounded by a summable function on $\partial S \mathrm{M}$ which does not depend on $\rho$.\\
For $(x,\xi)\in \partial S\mathrm{M}$, we put
$$
\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u =\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u -\langle\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u ,\nu\rangle\nu,\quad \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u =\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u -\langle\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u,\xi\rangle\xi.
$$  
We see that
$$
\langle\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u ,\nu\rangle=\langle\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u,\xi\rangle=0.
$$
Then $\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}$ and $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}$ are in fact  differential operators on $\partial S\mathrm{M}$ and $\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}u$, $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}u$ are completely determined by the restriction $u_{|\partial S\mathrm{M}}$ of $u$ on $\partial S\mathrm{M}$.\\
For $(x,\xi)\in\partial S\mathrm{M}$, by a simple computation we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{2.48}
\langle V, \nu \rangle=\langle \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u , \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u  \rangle\langle\xi,\nu\rangle-\langle \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u , \xi\rangle\langle \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}  u ,\nu\rangle.
\end{equation}
From (\ref{2.34}), we can see that the derivatives $\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}u$ and $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u$  are locally bounded on $\partial S\mathrm{M}$. It is important that the right-hand side of (\ref{2.48}) does not contain $\langle\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u,\nu\rangle$ and $\langle\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}u,\xi \rangle.$\\
Taking $\rho \rightarrow 0$ in the equality (\ref{2.46}), we have 
$$
\int_{S\mathrm{M}} \left[ \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2-\langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle+
(n-2) \vert Hu\vert ^2 \right]\,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}= -\int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}} \langle V, \nu \rangle \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}.
$$
Finally, It remains to prove the estimate (\ref{2.39}).  In view of the boundary condition $u=\mathcal{I} f$ on $\partial_+S\mathrm{M}$ and $u=0$ on $\partial_-S\mathrm{M}$ we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}} \langle V, \nu \rangle \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} &=\int_{\partial_+ S\mathrm{M}} \para{\langle \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} (\mathcal{I} f) , \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} (\mathcal{I} f)  \rangle\langle\xi,\nu\rangle-\langle \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} (\mathcal{I} f) , \xi\rangle\langle \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} (\mathcal{I} f) ,\nu\rangle} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}\cr
& :=\int_{\partial_+ S\mathrm{M}} \mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{I} f) \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} .
 \end{align*}
where $\mathcal{Q}u$ is a quadratic form in variables $\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}u$ and $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}u$ and hence, $\mathcal{Q}$ is a quadratic first-order  differential operator on the manifold $\partial_+ S \mathrm{M}$. Consequently, there exists a constant $C$ such that we have 
$$
\vert  \int_{\partial_+ S \mathrm{M}} \mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{I} f) \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} \vert \leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert ^2_{H^1(\partial_+ S \mathrm{M})}.
$$
 This completes the proof of the Theorem \ref{theorem}.

$$
P(\theta,\xi)=\frac{1-\abs{\theta}^2}{\alpha_n\abs{\theta-\xi}^n},\quad \theta\in B(0,1);\,\, \xi\in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
$$
For $0<\kappa<1$, we define $\Psi_\kappa: S_y\mathrm{M}_1\times S_y\mathrm{M}_1\to \mathbb{R}$ as
$$
\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi)=P(\kappa\theta,\xi).
$$
Let $P_0$ the Poisson kernel for the Euclidian unit ball $B_0(0,1)\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ i.e., 
$$
P_0(\hat{\theta},\hat{\xi})=\frac{1-\abs{\hat{\theta}}_0^2}{\alpha_n\abs{\hat{\theta}-\hat{\xi}}_0^n},\quad \hat{\theta}\in B_0(0,1);\,\, \hat{\xi}\in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}.
$$
where $\abs{\cdot}_0$ is the Euclidian norm of $\mathbb{R}^n$. From the well known properties of $P_0$, we have 
$$
\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}P_0(\kappa\hat{\theta},\hat{\xi}) d\omega_0(\hat{\xi})=1, \quad\textrm{for all}\, \kappa\in (0,1),\,\, \hat{\theta}\in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}.
$$
Let $\gamma=\sqrt{\mathrm{g}}:=(\gamma_{ij})$ be definite symetric positive matrix such that $\gamma^2=(g_{ij})$, then we get
$$
P(\theta,\xi)=\frac{1-\abs{\gamma^{-1}\theta}_0^2}{\alpha_n\abs{\gamma^{-1}\theta-\gamma^{-1}\xi}_0^n},\quad \theta,\xi\in S_y\mathrm{M}.
$$
we deduce from the change of variable $\hat{\xi}=\gamma^{-1}\xi$
\begin{eqnarray}\label{A1}
\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}P(\kappa\theta,\xi)d\omega_y(\xi)&=&\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}P_0(\kappa\gamma^{-1}\theta,\gamma^{-1}\xi)d\omega_y(\xi)\cr
&=&\frac{1}{\det\gamma}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}P_0(\kappa\gamma^{-1}\theta,\hat{\xi})(\det\gamma) d\omega_0(\hat{\xi})=1
\end{eqnarray}
This complete the proof of (\ref{4.18}).
Let now
$$
V_\theta=\set{\xi\in S_y\mathrm{M}_1,\,\,\abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}\leq (1-\kappa)^{1/2n}}.
$$
\begin{multline}\label{A.2}

(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}+4(1-\kappa)^{1/2}+(1-\kappa)\leq C(1-\kappa)^{1/2n},

and then we get (\ref{4.19}).\\
By a simple computation, we have
$$

we deduce that

Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold
\setcounter{equation}{0}


The geodesic $X$-ray transform of a function is defined by integrating over geodesics.
It is naturally arises in linearization of the problem of determining a coefficient in partial differential equation. The $X$-ray transform also
arises in Computer Tomography, Positron Emission Tomography, geophysical imaging
in determining the inner structure of the Earth, ultrasound imaging. Uniqueness
result and stability estimates of the geodesic $X$-ray transform were obtained by Mukhometov \cite{[Mukh]} for simple surface. For simple manifolds of any dimension this
result was proven in \cite{[SU2]}, \cite{[SU3]}, see also V. A. Sharafutdinov's book \cite{[Sh]}. In his paper Dairbekov generalized this result for nontrapping manifolds without conjugate points \cite{[Dai]}. Fredholm type inversion formulas were given in \cite{[PU]} by Pestov and Uhlmann.
\medskip

In this section we first collect some  formulas needed in the rest of this paper and introduce the geodesical $X$-ray transform on the manifolds we will be using. Let $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ be a Riemannian manifold, for $x\in \mathrm{M}$ and $\xi\in T_x\mathrm{M}$ we let  $\gamma_{x,\xi}$ denote the unique geodesic starting at the point $x$ in the direction $\xi$.  By
\begin{align*}
S\mathrm{M}=\set{(x,\xi)\in T\mathrm{M};\,\abs{\xi}=1}, \quad
S^*\mathrm{M}=\set{(x,p)\in T^*\mathrm{M};\,\abs{p}=1},
\end{align*}
we denote the sphere bundle and co-sphere bundle of $\mathrm{M}$. The exponential map $\exp_x:T_x\mathrm{M}\to \mathrm{M}$ is given by
\begin{equation}\label{2.1}
\exp_x(v)=\gamma_{x,\xi}(\abs{v}),\quad \xi=\frac{v\,\,}{\abs{v}}.
\end{equation}
A compact Riemannian manifold $(\mathrm{M},\, \mathrm{g})$ with boundary is called a convex non-trapping
manifold, if it satisfies two conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] the boundary $\partial \mathrm{M}$ is strictly convex, i.e., the second fundamental form of the boundary is positive definite at every
    boundary point,
    \item[(ii)] all geodesics having finite length in $\mathrm{M}$, i.e., for each $(x,\xi) \in S\mathrm{M}$, the maximal
    geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)$ satisfying the initial conditions $\gamma_{x,\xi}(0) = x$ and $\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(0) = \xi$ is defined on
    a finite segment with extremities $\ell_{-}(x,\xi)$ and $\ell_{+}(x,\xi)$. We recall that a geodesic $\gamma: [a, b] \longrightarrow M$ is maximal
    if it cannot be extended to a segment $[a-\varepsilon_1, b+\varepsilon_2]$, where $\varepsilon_i \geq 0$ and $\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 > 0$.
\end{enumerate}
An important subclass of convex non-trapping manifolds are simple manifolds. We say that a compact Riemannian
manifold $(\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{g})$ is simple if it satisfies the following properties
\begin{enumerate}
     \item[(a)] $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ is convex and non-trapping, 
     \item[(b)] there are no conjugate points on any geodesic.
\end{enumerate}
A simple $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold is diffeomorphic to a closed ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and any pair of
points in the manifold are joined by an unique geodesic.
\medskip

Let $(x,\xi)\in S\mathrm{M}$, there exist a unique geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}$ associated to $(x,\xi)$ which is maxmimally defined on a finite intervall $[\ell_-(x,\xi),\ell_+(x,\xi)]$, with $\gamma_{x,\xi}(\ell_\pm(x,\xi))\in\partial\mathrm{M}$. We define the geodesic flow $\phi_t$ as following
\begin{equation}\label{2.2}
\phi_t:S\mathrm{M}\to S\mathrm{M},\quad \phi_t(x,\xi)=(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(t)),\quad t\in [\ell_-(x,\xi),\ell_+(x,\xi)],
\end{equation}
and $\phi_t$ is a flow, that is, $\phi_t\circ\phi_s=\phi_{t+s}$.
\smallskip

Now, we introduce the submanifolds of inner and outer vectors of $S\mathrm{M}$
\begin{equation}\label{2.3}
\partial_{\pm}S\mathrm{M} =\set{(x,\xi)\in S\mathrm{M},\, x \in \partial \mathrm{M},\, \pm\seq{\xi,\nu(x)}< 0},
\end{equation}
where $\nu$ is the unit outer normal to the boundary. Note that the manifolds $\partial_+ S\mathrm{M}$ and $\partial_-S\mathrm{M}$ have the same boundary $S(\partial \mathrm{M})$, and $\partial S\mathrm{M} = \partial_+ S\mathrm{M}\cup \partial_- S\mathrm{M}$. We denote by  $\mathcal{C}^\infty(\partial_+ S\mathrm{M})$ be space of smooth functions on the manifold $\partial_+S\mathrm{M}$. Thus we can define two functions $\ell_\pm:S\mathrm{M}\to\mathbb{R}$ which satisfy
$$
\ell_-(x,\xi)\leq 0,\quad \ell_+(x,\xi)\geq 0,\quad \ell_+(x,\xi)=-\ell_-(x,-\xi),
$$
$$
\ell_-(x,\xi)=0,\quad (x,\xi)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M},\quad \ell_+(x,\xi)=0,\quad (x,\xi)\in\partial_-S\mathrm{M},
$$
$$
\ell_-(\phi_t(x,\xi))=\ell_-(x,\xi)-t,\quad \ell_+(\phi_t(x,\xi))=\ell_+(x,\xi)-t.
$$
For $(x,\xi)\in\partial_+ S\mathrm{M}$,  we denote by $\gamma_{x,\xi} : [0,\ell_+(x,\xi)] \to \mathrm{M}$ the maximal
geodesic satisfying the initial conditions $\gamma_{x,\xi}(0) = x$ and $\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(0) = \xi$.

\smallskip

Concerning smoothness properties of  $\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$, we can see that these functions are smooth near a point $(x,\xi)$ such that the geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)$ intersects $\partial\mathrm{M}$ transversely for $t=\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$. By strict convexity of $\partial\mathrm{M}$, the functions $\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$ are smooth on $T\mathrm{M} \setminus T(\partial\mathrm{M}).$ In fact, all points of $T\mathrm{M} \cap T(\partial\mathrm{M})$ are singular for $\ell_{\pm}$; since some derivatives of these functions are unbounded in a neighbourhood of such points. In particular, $\ell_{+}$ is smooth on $\partial_+SM$, see Lemma 4.1.1 of \cite{[Sh]}.
\smallskip


The Riemannian scalar product on $T_x\mathrm{M}$ induces the volume form on $S_x\mathrm{M}$,
denoted by $\mathrm{d} \omega_x(\xi)$ and given by
$$
\mathrm{d} \omega_x(\xi)=\sqrt{\abs{\mathrm{g}}} \, \sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^k\xi^k \mathrm{d} \xi^1\wedge\cdots\wedge \widehat{\mathrm{d} \xi^k}\wedge\cdots\wedge \mathrm{d} \xi^n.
$$
As usual, the notation $\, \widehat{\cdot} \,$ means that the corresponding factor has been dropped.
We introduce the volume form $\,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}$ on the manifold $S\mathrm{M}$ by
$$
\,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} (x,\xi)=\mathrm{d}\omega_x(\xi)\wedge \,\mathrm{dv}^{n},
$$
where $\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}$ is the Riemannnian volume form on $\mathrm{M}$. By Liouville's theorem, the form $\,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}$ is preserved by the geodesic flow. The
corresponding volume form on the boundary $\partial S\mathrm{M} =\set{(x,\xi)\in S\mathrm{M},\, x\in\partial \mathrm{M}}$ is given
by
$$
\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}=\mathrm{d}\omega_x(\xi) \wedge \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1},
$$
where $\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1}$ is the volume form of $\partial \mathrm{M}$.
\smallskip


Let $L^2_\mu(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})$ be the space of square integrable functions with respect to the measure $\mu(x,\xi)\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}$ with
$\mu(x,\xi)=\abs{\seq{\xi,\nu(x)}}$. This Hilbert space is endowed with the scalar product
\begin{equation}\label{2.4}
\para{u,v}_\mu=\int_{\partial_+S\mathrm{M}}u(x,\xi) \overline{v}(x,\xi) \mu(x,\xi)\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}.
\end{equation}
The ray transform (also called geodesic $X$-ray transform) on a convex non trapping manifold $\mathrm{M}$ is the linear operator
\begin{equation}\label{2.5}
\mathcal{I}:\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathrm{M})\longrightarrow \mathcal{C}^\infty(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}),
\end{equation}
defined by the equality
\begin{equation}\label{2.6}
\mathcal{I} f(x,\xi)=\int_0^{\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t))\, \mathrm{d} t,\quad (x,\xi)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}.
\end{equation}
The right-hand side of (\ref{2.6}) is a smooth function on $\partial_+S\mathrm{M}$ because the integration limit $\ell_+(x,\xi)$ is a smooth function on $\partial_+S\mathrm{M}$.
The ray transform on a convex non trapping manifold $\mathrm{M}$ can be extended as a bounded operator
\begin{equation}\label{2.7}
\mathcal{I}:H^k(\mathrm{M})\longrightarrow H^k(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}),
\end{equation}
for every integer $k\geq 1$, see Theorem 4.2.1 of \cite{[Sh]}.
\medskip

Preliminary estimates
The main purpose of this section is to present a preliminary estimate, which relates the
difference of two absorption coefficients to the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map.
As before, we let $a_1,\,a_2\in\mathscr{A}(m_1,\eta)$ and $q_1,q_2\in\mathscr{Q}(m_2)$ such that $a_1=a_2$, $q_1=q_2$ near  the boundary $\partial\mathrm{M}$. We set
$$
a(x)=(a_1-a_2)(x),\quad q(x)=(q_1-q_2)(x).
$$
Recall that we have extended $a_{1},a_{2}$ as $W^{2,\infty}(\mathrm{M}_1)$ in such a way that $a=0$ and $q=0$ on $\mathrm{M}_{1} \setminus \mathrm{M}$.\\
We denote $\psi_{a_2}\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ and $\psi_{-a_1}\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ the solutions of (\ref{3.12}) respectively with $a=a_2$ and $a=-a_1$ given by (\ref{3.22}), and set
\begin{equation}\label{4.1}
\psi_a(x,t)=\psi_{a_2}(x,t)\psi_{-a_1}(x,t).
\end{equation} 
\begin{lemma}\label{L.4.1}
Let $T>0$. There exist $C>0$ such that for any $\theta_j\in \mathcal{V}(Q)$, $j=1,2$, 
satisfying the transport equation (\ref{3.7}), the following estimate holds true:
\begin{equation}\label{4.2}
\abs{\int_{0}^T\!\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}}a(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)\psi_{a}(x,t)\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t } 
\leq C\para{h+h^{-2}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}}\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}
\end{equation}
for all $h\in (0,h_0)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof} First, if $\theta_2$ satisfies (\ref{3.11}), $\psi_{a_2}$ satisfies (\ref{3.12}), and $h<h_0$, Lemma \ref{L.3.2} guarantees
the existence of a geometrical optics solution $u_2$
\begin{equation}\label{4.3}
u_2(x,t)=(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_{2,h}(x,t),
\end{equation}
to the wave equation corresponding to the coefficients $a_2$ and $q_2$,
$$
\para{\partial^2_t-\Delta+a_2(x)\partial_t+q_2(x)}u(x,t)=0\quad \textrm{in}\,Q, \quad u(\cdot,0)=\partial_tu(\cdot,0)=0 \quad \textrm{in}\,\, \mathrm{M},
$$
where $r_{2,h}$ satisfies
\begin{gather}\label{4.4}
h^{-1}\norm{r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{\partial_t r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{\nabla r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)},
\\ \nonumber
r_{2,h}(x,t)=0,\quad\forall (x,t)\in\,\Sigma.
\end{gather}
Moreover
$$
u_2\in  \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\mathrm{M})) \cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})).
$$
Let us denote by $f_h$ the function
$$
f_h(x,t)=(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h},\quad  (x,t)\in\Sigma,
$$
and we consider $v$ the solution of the following non-homogenous boundary value problem
\begin{equation}\label{4.5}
\left\{\begin{array}{lll}
\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)} v=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, Q,\cr
v(x,0)=\partial_tv(x,0)=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, \mathrm{M},\cr
v(x,t)=u_2(x,t):=f_{h}(x,t), & \textrm{on}\,\, \Sigma.
\end{array}
\right.
\end{equation}
We let $ w=v-u_2$. Therefore, $w$ solves the following homogenous boundary value problem
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{lll}
\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}w(x,t)=a(x)\partial_tu_2(x,t)+q(x)u_2(x,t) & \textrm{in}\,\,  Q,\cr
w(x,0)=\partial_tw(x,0)=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, \mathrm{M},\cr
w(x,t)=0, & \textrm{on}\,\,  \Sigma.
\end{array}
\right.
$$
Using the fact that  $a(x)\partial_tu_2+q(x)u_2 \in W^{1,1}(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))$ with $u_2(\cdot,0)=\partial_t u_2(\cdot,0)\equiv 0$, by Lemma \ref{L.1.1}, we deduce that
$$
w\in \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})\cap
H^1_0(\mathrm{M})).
$$
Therefore, we have constructed a special solution
  $$ 
  \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\mathrm{M})) \cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})),
  $$
to the backward wave equation
\begin{align*}
\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta-a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}u_1(x,t)&=0,  \quad (x,t) \in Q, \\
u_1(x,T)=u_1(x,T)&=0,  \quad x \in \mathrm{M},
\end{align*}
having the special form
\begin{equation}\label{4.6}
u_1(x,t)=(\theta_1\psi_{-a_1})( t,x)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_{1,h}(x,t),
\end{equation}
which corresponds to the coefficients $-a_1$ and $q_1$, where
$r_{1,h}$ satisfies for $h<h_0$
\begin{equation}\label{4.7}
h^{-1}\norm{r_{1,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{\partial_t r_{1,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{\nabla
r_{1,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
\end{equation}
Integrating by parts and using Green's formula (\ref{3.4}), we find
\begin{multline}\label{4.8}
\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M}\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}w\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t
= \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tu_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t
=-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \partial_\nu w\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t.
\end{multline}
Taking (\ref{4.8}), (\ref{4.6}) into account, we deduce
\begin{multline}\label{4.9}
-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tu_2\overline{u}_1(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\,\mathrm{d} t 
=\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}}\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2,q_2}} f_{h}(x,t)\overline{g}_h(x,t) \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t
\end{multline}
where $g_h$ is given by
$$
g_h(x,t)=(\theta_1\psi_{-a_1})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h},\quad (x,t)\in \Sigma.
$$
It follows from (\ref{4.9}), (\ref{4.6}) and (\ref{4.3}) that
\begin{multline}\label{4.10}
ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\theta_2 \overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)(\psi_{a_2}\psi_{-a_1})( x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\,\mathrm{d} t =\cr
\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t
-ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(t,x)e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t r_{2,h}(\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1})(x,t) e^{-i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tr_{2,h}(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2(x,t)\overline{u}_1(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt \cr
= \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h \para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t+\mathscr{R}_h.
\end{multline}
In view of (\ref{4.7}) and (\ref{4.4}), we have
\begin{equation}\label{4.11}
\abs{\mathscr{R}_h}\leq C\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, by the trace theorem, we find
\begin{eqnarray}\label{4.12}
\bigg|\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}}\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}(f_{h}) \overline{g}_h \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t \bigg|
&\leq & \norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}} \norm{f_h}_{H^{1}(\Sigma)}\norm{g_h}_{L^2(\Sigma)}\cr
&\leq & Ch^{-3}\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}
-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}.
\end{eqnarray}
The estimate (\ref{4.2}) follows easily from (\ref{4.10}), (\ref{4.11}) and (\ref{4.12}).\\
This completes the proof of the Lemma.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{L.4.2} There exists $C>0$ such that for any $\Psi\in H^2 (S_y\mathrm{M}_{1})$, the following estimate
\begin{multline}\label{4.13}
\abs{\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\para{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)}-1}
\Psi(\xi)  \,  
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)}\cr
 \leq C\para{h+h^{-2}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}} \norm{\Psi}_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_{1})}.
\end{multline}
holds for any $y\in\partial\mathrm{M}_1$.
\end{lemma}
We use the notation
    $$ S_y^+\mathrm{M}_{1} = \big\{\xi \in S_{y}\mathrm{M}_{1} : \langle \nu,\xi \rangle<0 \big\}. $$
\begin{proof}
We take two solutions to (\ref{3.11}) of the form
\begin{align*}
\widetilde{\theta}_1(t,r,\xi)&=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi), \\
\widetilde{\theta}_2(t,r,\xi)&=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r).
\end{align*}
Now we change variable in the left term of (\ref{4.1}), $x=\exp_{y}(r\xi)$, $r>0$ and
$\xi\in S_{y}\mathrm{M}_1$, we have
\begin{multline}\label{4.14}
\int_0^T\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\overline{\theta}_1\theta_2)(x,t)\psi_{a}(x,t)  \,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t \cr
=\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)(\overline{\widetilde{\theta}}_1\widetilde{\theta}_2)( t,r,\xi)
\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t,r,\xi)
\alpha^{1/2} \, \mathrm{d} r \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t\cr
=\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)\phi^2( t-r)\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t,r,\xi)\Psi(\xi)  \, \mathrm{d} r \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)
\, \mathrm{d} t\cr
=\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_\mathbb{R} \widetilde{a}( t-\tau,y,\xi)\phi^2(\tau)\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t, t-\tau,\xi)\Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)
\, \mathrm{d} t\cr
=\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_\mathbb{R} \widetilde{a}( t-\tau,y,\xi)\phi^2(\tau)\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ t}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}
\Psi(\xi)  \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)\cr
=2\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\int_0^T \frac{d}{dt}\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ t}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}
\Psi(\xi)  \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)\cr
=2\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ T}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}-1}
\Psi(\xi)  \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi).
\end{multline}
By the support properties of the function $\phi$, we get that the left-hand side term in (\ref{4.14}) reads
\begin{multline*}
  \int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{T}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}-1}
\Psi(\xi)  \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)=\cr
\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(s,y,\xi)ds}-1}
\Psi(\xi) \mu(y,\xi) \, 
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi).
\end{multline*}
Then, by (\ref{4.14}) and (\ref{4.2}) we get
\begin{multline}\label{4.15}
\abs{\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\para{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)}-1}
\Psi(\xi)  \,  
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)}\cr
 \leq C\para{h+h^{-2}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}} \norm{\Psi}_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_{1})}.
\end{multline}
This completes the proof of the Lemma.
\end{proof}
